docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
How Newmota is built, in one page: the same portable application runs on five chip families by talking only through small native platform adapters — no Arduino layer, direct vendor SDKs. Contributors start here; users only need the takeaway that daily behavior (commands, web UI, templates) is identical everywhere, while flashing and recovery differ per chip.

docs.title: 1. Zero Host Fallback & Zero Arduino Core
docs.text: Newmota compiles directly against vendor SDKs (ESP-IDF, BouffaloSDK, LibreTiny framework-beken-bdk, Ameba RTOS). It does not use Arduino abstraction layers, host compiler mocks, or third-party application frameworks.

docs.title: 2. Platform Admission Requirement
docs.text: Sub-2 MiB physical flash devices are excluded from scope. Every target platform must provide at least 2 MiB of physical flash to run Newmota.

docs.title: 3. Public Platform Contract
docs.text: Portable code (src/app/) never includes native SDK headers directly. All platform interactions pass through src/platform/include/newmota/platform/ headers and the newmota::platform namespace: - System boot and shutdown lifecycle hooks. - System ticks and high-resolution timer access. - Console UART input/output (single application console for logs + commands). - Flash partition access and LittleFS VFS binding. - Native digital GPIO, Wi-Fi station, restart/safeboot mechanics, and (on ESP) the RTC fast-restart guard.

docs.title: 4. Native Entry Points
docs.text: Each platform owns its native startup entry point under src/platform/<platform>/native/: - Initializes vendor RTOS / hardware peripherals. - Mounts storage partitions. - Hands execution over to newmota::app::run().

docs.title: Porting References
docs.text:
Newmota migrates Tasmota behavior in small, independently buildable and testable slices:

  1. Tasmota is the primary behavioral and implementation reference. Every feature slice begins by reviewing the relevant Tasmota documentation and current source — even when Newmota will refactor substantially. The review identifies the compatibility contract, useful behavior, edge cases, and prior tradeoffs. Tasmota source is not copied as is; intentional differences and their rationale are recorded, and the Tasmota review remains a mandatory regression check.
  2. ESP-IDF is the leading Newmota implementation platform and the reference for common platform decisions. Other platforms normally follow the portable Newmota contract and the existing ESP-IDF/Newmota implementation.
  3. Fallback baseline: when neither Newmota nor Tasmota supplies a suitable implementation or configuration, the ESP-IDF/Tasmota configuration for the matching flash class is the default starting baseline — including partition layouts where practical. Native SDK boot constraints, image formats, alignment, reserved regions, and hardware evidence may require a deliberate deviation; the deviation is adapted deliberately and recorded rather than copied or guessed.

docs.title: Resource Profiles
docs.text:
Resource profiles are target build presets that define the feature set compiled into the binary.

Profile Target Flash Class Default Feature Surface Initial Targets Compact 2 MiB Flash Mandatory device-hosted web server + essential UI (HTTP+Gzip on port 80), bounded plain MQTT, LittleFS storage where the selected layout preserves it (Beken's OTA overlay may be erased), serial provisioning, basic I/O, Berry (mandatory in normal app builds). esp32c2-2m, pico-w, bl602-2m, cb2s-2m, bw16-2m Standard 4 MiB Flash All Compact features with more flash headroom: the crypto set Matter needs on ESP, and optional drivers (sensors, energy meters, WS2812, display). The web UI stays HTTP+Gzip by default; USE_WEB_HTTPS: true opts in. ESP32-C3/S3 reference, pico2-w Large 8 MiB+ Flash All Standard features, with HTTPS+Brotli web UI on port 443 (per-device self-signed certificate) enabled by default. Display, LVGL, and I2S audio are optional features that need the flash headroom. ESP32-P4, ESP32-S31, esp32s3-qio-opi-8m-8m Safeboot Recovery partition budget from the platform layout Minimal recovery image without the normal UI, Berry, time service, timers, or dev self-tests; carries a stripped authenticated HTTP+Gzip recovery page with a bounded application-image updater. Selected only by a safeboot-role environment, never a board default. bw16-2m-safeboot, esp32s3-qio-qspi-safeboot, bl602-2m-safeboot, pico-w-safeboot, pico2-w-safeboot

Warning

The profile follows the flash size on every platform: 2 MiB environments are Compact, 4 MiB environments Standard, and environments with 8 MiB or more Large. The one exception today is esp32h2, a 4 MiB environment with the Compact profile. make list shows the profile of every environment.

docs.title: Feature selection and experimental surfaces
docs.text: A feature compiled into a profile and a feature enabled by default are different things. BLE (USE_BLE, USE_BLE_SENSORS) and Matter (USE_MATTER, USE_MATTER_BLE, USE_MATTER_BRIDGE) are implemented but no checked-in profile selects them; enable them in a personal build and test on your hardware. See Personal Build Configurations.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Terms that the Newmota documentation uses. Many come from Tasmota and mean the same there; the ones that are new to Newmota are marked (Newmota).

Term Meaning Berry The scripting language built into every normal image, the same language Tasmota uses. See Berry Scripting. Board recipe (Newmota) The description of one board in the catalog: chip, flash, pins the board reserves. Several environments can use one board recipe. Environment (Newmota) A checked-in build target, such as esp32c3-4m or cb2s-2m: chip, board, flash layout, profile, language and features. make list shows them all. Factory package (Newmota) Everything a first flash over a cable needs, with a manifest that lists each file, where it goes and its hash. It is also packed as newmota-<environment>-<version>-factory.zip for the Web Flasher. Feature An optional part of the firmware, named USE_… as in Tasmota, for example USE_BME280. Features are chosen when the image is built, with make config. LittleFS The filesystem on the device's flash. Newmota keeps its settings in /.newmota/ and your files, such as autoexec.be, next to them. See Files & Settings. make config (Newmota) The interactive configurator that creates a personal build. See Build Your Firmware. Manifest (Newmota) The manifest.json of a build. Every flash and update command checks it and its hashes before it opens the device. OTA image The application image for an update over the network, in the build's ota/ folder. Personal build (Newmota) Your own configuration in user_config/<name>.yaml, based on an environment. git ignores it. See Personal Build Configurations. Platform A chip family with its vendor SDK: ESP-IDF, Pico SDK, Beken, Bouffalo or AmebaD. Profile (Newmota) The feature set an environment starts from, by flash size: Compact (2 MiB), Standard (4 MiB), Large (8 MiB or more). See Resource Profiles. Safeboot A small recovery image in its own partition, as in Tasmota. Restart 3 starts it; its web page accepts a new application image. Every Newmota application has a paired Safeboot. SetOption Numbered on/off and value settings with Tasmota's numbering and meaning, such as SetOption19. Slot A position in a template's GPIO list. It is not always the same as the GPIO number, because chips can have gaps in their numbering. See Setting Up Your Device Hardware. Solidify Building a Berry driver class into flash, so it needs no upload and no heap. Set in a personal build with solidify. Template The JSON description of which function sits on which pin, in Tasmota's format and with Tasmota's function numbers.

docs.title: Roadmap and Release Stages
docs.text:
Draft

This page is a draft. The stage boundaries are set; the conditions for moving from one stage to the next are proposals.

Newmota's version number tells you how far you can trust a build. The version is shown in the boot log, in Status 2 ("Version") and in the web interface.

No stage makes over-the-air updates safe

Newmota does not promise that an over-the-air update succeeds, in any stage, stable included; no firmware project can. A power cut, a weak Wi-Fi link, a flash fault or a bug can leave a device that only a wired flash brings back. Before you install Newmota on a device, know how you would flash it over a wire, and keep a backup of the original firmware and your settings.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text: Version Stage Use it on 0.0.x Pre-alpha Development boards only 0.1 – 0.7.x Alpha Devices you can easily flash over a wire again 0.8 – 0.9.x Beta Everyday devices, but expect frequent problems 1.0 and later Stable Normal use

docs.title: Pre-alpha (0.0.x)
docs.text: There is no real release yet. Every build is 0.0.1, so two builds with the same number can differ completely. Commands, settings and file formats can change at any time, and an update can lose the device's settings. Use a development board with a USB serial port.

docs.title: Alpha (0.1 – 0.7.x)
docs.text: Releases have their own version numbers. Features still change, and settings and file formats can still change from one release to the next. An over-the-air update or the recovery path can fail and leave the device needing a wired flash, so only use devices whose serial pins you can reach easily.

docs.title: Beta (0.8 – 0.9.x)
docs.text: Features are mostly complete, and over-the-air updates and Safeboot recovery have been tested on every supported family. Bugs are still frequent, so keep a backup of the original firmware and your settings.

docs.title: Stable (1.0 and later)
docs.text: Updates within a major version keep your settings and commands working. An over-the-air update can still fail; see the warning at the top of this page.

docs.title: Rough timeline
docs.text:
A target, not a promise; dates move when the conditions below are not met.

Stage Target Alpha (0.1) January 2027 Beta (0.8) March 2027 Stable (1.0) January 2028

docs.title: Pre-alpha to alpha (0.1)
docs.text:
• A release is built from a tagged commit, and its packages carry that version.
  • On at least one board for each platform family (ESP32, Beken, Bouffalo, Raspberry Pi Pico, AmebaD), the core passes a hardware test: boot and restart, Wi-Fi, web interface, console, MQTT, the file system, and a wired factory flash.

docs.title: Alpha to beta (0.8)
docs.text:
• Over-the-air update and Safeboot recovery pass hardware tests on every supported family, including power loss during an update.
  • The open hardware checks for the features in the default builds are done.

docs.title: Beta to stable (1.0)
docs.text:
• The settings and file formats are fixed, and commands keep their meaning within the major version.
  • No known problem leaves a device unrecoverable without a wire.

docs.title: Coming from Tasmota
docs.text:
Newmota treats Tasmota as its behavioral reference: every feature starts from Tasmota's documentation and current source, and deviations are deliberate and recorded. If you arrive from Tasmota, most of your muscle memory transfers — this page lists what doesn't. To move a device, see Switching From Tasmota.

Newmota is an independent project. It is not part of, affiliated with or endorsed by Tasmota or OpenBeken, so please report problems with Newmota to the Newmota project and not to them. Newmota owes a lot to both: Tasmota for the commands, templates and Berry integration it follows, and OpenBeken for its work on Beken and other Tuya-module chips.

Building your own image

Tasmota offers ready-made binaries for most devices and tailored builds through user_config_override.h. Newmota has no downloads yet, so you build your own image, and make config makes that easy: pick your chip and features from a menu, and Newmota checks the combination before it compiles. See Build Your Firmware.

docs.title: What carries over unchanged
docs.text:
• Console habits: case-insensitive commands, JSON replies, the _ quiet prefix, ? queries.
  • Status 1/2/3/4/5/7/8/10/11 telemetry sections and their JSON shapes.
  • SetOption0…177 numbering and boolean/parameter semantics.
  • Wi-Fi slots (SSId1/Password1, SSId2/Password2), Timezone/TimeStd/TimeDst/NtpServer, SerialLog/WebLog numbering.
  • Module / Template / GPIO workflow, template JSON shape, and the frozen 16-bit GPIO function IDs. Per-pin GPIO overrides still apply only to User slots.
  • Power stack: Power, PowerOnState 0…5, PulseTime, BlinkTime/BlinkCount, Interlock.
  • Light stack: Dimmer, Channel, Color, CT, White, HsbColor, Fade, Speed, LedTable, Scheme 0..14, Wakeup.
  • Sensors: StatusSNS, MQTT tele/<topic>/SENSOR, SetOption8 (°C/°F), SetOption24/SetOption139 (pressure units), TempRes/HumRes/PressRes, TempOffset/HumOffset.
  • MQTT topic convention: cmnd/<topic>/#, stat/<topic>/RESULT, stat/<topic>/POWER, tele/<topic>/STATE, tele/<topic>/SENSOR.
  • Reset 1…6 meanings (including keep-Wi-Fi variants 4–6) and Restart 1 / Restart 99.
  • Berry: the Br command, /autoexec.be startup script, and SetOption153 to disable it. Berry runs in every normal build — including small 2 MiB Compact devices.
  • WebPassword exists and behaves the Tasmota way.

Note

A feature that is not implemented yet belongs under current gaps, not in the deliberate-differences table.

Compatibility lives at the command, data and device-behavior edges; the internal driver and build structure is Newmota's own.

docs.title: Current gaps that are not deliberate differences
docs.text:
These items are intended to follow Tasmota or the approved Newmota design once implementation and testing are complete:

  • TLS: HTTPS for the normal web service and TLS MQTT. The current Compact slice uses authenticated HTTP+Gzip because it is the measured implementation available today.
  • Recovery: the separate Safeboot browser updater, remote update, failed-boot handling, and platform-specific recovery testing.
  • Button debounce: ButtonDebounce supports the normal 10 ms filter and logical HIGH/LOW stability flags. The native 2 ms AC pulse detector selected by values ending in 9 remains open; those values are explicitly rejected. Cooperative probes can be delayed by blocking application work.
  • Returning to stock Tasmota remains a separate optional gate.
  • Ping: Wi-Fi applications include asynchronous IPv4 ICMP Ping; Safeboot omits it. Newmota permits one fixed campaign, uses asynchronous DNS, and accepts indices 0–8 (default one; zero tries up to four and stops at the first reply). It rejects larger indices, IPv6, whitespace and ambiguous numeric address spellings. Tasmota can keep campaigns for multiple destinations and supports IPv6 when selected. Newmota's five-second DNS deadline, one-second probe deadline/cadence, busy state through cancellation/delivery, and queryable current/last status are deliberate bounds. Results retain numeric counters on DNS failure and add an Error field. Host tests and native compilation do not establish device reachability.
  • Additional drivers and commands whose platform owners do not yet exist.
  • Audio consumers: TensorFlow microphone integration, camera/audio synchronization, simultaneous network walkie-talkie routing and BLE audio endpoints. The native session API supports bounded microphone capture, encoded files/network streams and configurable I2S input/output, but these higher-level consumers have no Newmota owners.
  • Berry Light timer callbacks; light.get()/light.set() cover retained endpoint state and synchronous mutations, and the gamma helpers provide pure integer conversions.
  • Matter follow-up: access-control/CASE enforcement, production attestation, MtrUpdate, and testing beyond a first commissioning.
  • Module2 and other unfinished compatibility edges.
  • Further MQTT features: Home Assistant discovery for lights, switches and buttons, Rules, and MQTT file/log streaming.
  • Stock Tasmota-to-Newmota OTA migration: a bootstrap settings importer is present in ESP32 source for all eight ESP targets; end-to-end device trials remain open. See Switching From Tasmota.

docs.title: Berry filesystem listings
docs.text: Berry path.listdir() returns direct-child basenames with a deliberate limit of 128 entries and 8192 bytes of names per call. Exceeding either limit raises value_error without returning a partial listing. Paths use the shared filesystem limit of 191 bytes and reject embedded NUL bytes.

docs.title: Build From Source
docs.text: Contributor reference for compiling Newmota: environment, board catalog, toolchains, test matrices and build variables. To configure and build an image for your own device, start with Build Your Firmware.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• macOS or Linux host system.
  • Python 3.10+ installed.
  • uv package manager installed (uv installation guide).
  • Standard build utilities: make, git, and optionally ccache for build acceleration.

docs.title: 1. Setup Environment
docs.text:
Initialize the project Python environment managed by uv:

make uv-setup

This creates the isolated .venv directory and installs the lockfile-pinned helper tools (pyserial, littlefs-python, pyyaml, bk7231tools, blflashcommand, and more).

docs.title: 2. Inspect the Catalog
docs.text:
Inspect configured hardware targets, environment files, and board recipes:

# List all configured chips, boards, and environments
make list

# Open the menuconfig/configurator for a personal build
make config

Validate the complete declarative catalog without compiling firmware or installing heavy platform SDKs:

make validate-catalog

docs.title: 3. Toolchain & SDK Setup
docs.text:
Platform toolchains and native SDK dependencies can be installed explicitly or fetched lazily on first build.

# Install tools for a specific target environment
make setup ENV=esp32c2-2m

# Or install all tools for an entire platform cohort
make setup PLATFORM=esp
make setup PLATFORM=bouffalo
make setup PLATFORM=beken
make setup PLATFORM=amebad
make setup PLATFORM=pico
make setup PLATFORM=all

# Verify the installed SDKs against config/sdk/*.toml
make sdk-check

Note

Toolchains are installed outside the project tree (e.g. ~/.espressif for ESP-IDF and ~/.newmota/tools/ for other platforms) using host Python interpreters to prevent virtualenv contamination.

docs.title: 4. Building Firmware
docs.text:
Build an individual environment:

# Build the baseline ESP32-C2 2 MiB environment
make esp32c2-2m

# Or build the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W environment
make pico2-w

# Or using the explicit build target form
make build ENV=esp32c2-2m

Build any target board recipe on demand, independently of the test matrix:

make esp32s3-qio-opi

Board recipes are also generated Make targets. ESP-IDF has an environment for every board recipe, so make all builds the complete ESP-IDF set while make test remains the five-entry routine matrix. Direct board builds resolve the same-named environment when one exists and run lazy SDK setup.

Build the checked-in cross-platform test matrix defined in config/env/matrices/test.txt (4 Compact 2 MiB environments + 1 Standard 4 MiB Pico 2 W target: esp32c2-2m, bl602-2m, cb2s-2m, bw16-2m, pico2-w):

make test

Run host tests and primitive cryptographic known-answer suites:

make test-host

Build all configured environments (this takes a very long time; the routine check is make test):

make all JOBS=8

docs.title: Build variables
docs.text:
Variable Effect JOBS=<n> Parallel jobs; default is every logical CPU. Beken's Make-based build always uses one. VERBOSE=1 Shows native compiler commands and full SDK output (NEWMOTA_VERBOSE=1 for the CLI). SDK_LOG_LEVEL=<level> Vendor SDK log level: none, error, warn (default), info, debug, verbose.

Native SDK work goes to build/work/<environment>/; packages with their manifest go to build/firmware/<environment>/<version>/. Pico builds also write a UF2 below build/work/<environment>/native/. make format-cpp formats the first-party C/C++ sources with the pinned formatter (make format-check-cpp checks), and make clangd ENV=<env> writes a compilation database for editors.

docs.title: 5. Personal Configurations
docs.text:
You can create local, custom build definitions without modifying checked-in files by creating user_config/<custom-id>.yaml and inheriting from an existing environment. Build your custom environment with:

make <custom-id>

See Personal Build Configurations for full details on supported overrides (profile, language, crypto, native).

docs.title: 6. Next Steps
docs.text:
• Explore Install & Update Firmware to probe, backup, or flash hardware.
  • Set up Editor Support for your IDE.
  • Inspect the Console & Commands reference for serial device interactions.

docs.title: Build System Internals
docs.text: Newmota provides a single, unified command interface driven by a top-level Makefile and Python build orchestration scripts (tools/newmota/). This page is contributor reference — if you just want firmware for your device, see Install & Update Firmware.

docs.title: Core Architecture
docs.text:
Rather than relying on separate build systems for each micro-controller vendor, Newmota defines a common pipeline interface that maps platform-specific setup, configuration, compilation, and packaging tasks into standardized execution steps.

flowchart LR
    User["Developer / CI"] -->|make env| Makefile["Top-Level Makefile"]
    Makefile -->|python -m newmota| Driver["Build Orchestration Driver"]
    Driver --> Catalog["Catalog Resolver<br/>(chips, boards, envs)"]
    Driver --> PlatformAdapter["Platform Adapter<br/>(platforms/esp, pico, bouffalo, beken, amebad)"]
    PlatformAdapter --> NativeSDK["Native Upstream SDK Build System"]

make forwards to the unified python -m newmota CLI (tools/newmota/__main__.py). Each platforms/<platform>/ directory owns its build.py (setup/build), images.py (layout/packaging), and device.py (programmer protocol) — see the source layout and the build-tool ownership guide linked there.

docs.title: Command Interface Summary
docs.text: Command Description make uv-setup Creates and synchronizes Python virtual environment with uv. make list Lists all configured chips, boards, and environments. make config Opens the interactive configurator, writes a personal user_config/<name>.yaml, and can build it. make validate-catalog Runs comprehensive validation on declarative configuration files. make setup ENV=<name> Installs missing cross-compiler toolchains and SDK dependencies for a target. make setup PLATFORM=<name> Installs toolchains for an entire platform cohort (esp, pico, bouffalo, beken, amebad, all). make sdk-check Verifies the installed SDKs (release archives or .sdk/ checkouts) against the pins in config/sdk/. make sdk-fetch Downloads every pinned SDK release archive, for offline builds. make sdk-checkout SDK=<key> Clones a pinned SDK into .sdk/ for SDK patch work; builds then use that checkout. make <environment> Builds a specific target environment (e.g. make esp32c2-2m, make pico2-w). make build BOARD=<name> Builds any native board recipe on demand (e.g. make esp32s3-qio-opi). make test Builds the five-entry cross-platform routine test matrix (esp32c2-2m, bl602-2m, cb2s-2m, bw16-2m, pico2-w). make test-host Runs host-side crypto KAT suites and Berry VM across all, partial, and no-crypto build profiles. Does not require device hardware. make all JOBS=8 Builds every environment defined under config/env/ (including all ESP-IDF targets). make clangd ENV=<name> Generates editor compilation database for target.

docs.title: Device Operations in Detail
docs.text: Every device command validates the package manifest and all SHA-256 hashes before it opens a serial connection.

docs.title: What make update writes
docs.text:
make update is the short wired development cycle — it is not the signed remote OTA implementation. It is implemented for ESP-IDF and has wired paths for Beken, AmebaD, Bouffalo, and Pico:

  • ESP-IDF: invokes the application-only build and writes only app0; bootloader, partition table, Safeboot, OTA-selection data, and LittleFS are neither rebuilt nor written.
  • AmebaD: runs the SDK's coupled KM0/KM4 build and writes only the combined application image to OTA2. That SDK build may regenerate boot-image side outputs, but make update does not write them and does not build Safeboot or a filesystem package. Since boot selection is preserved, a device currently in Safeboot remains there.
  • Beken: writes only the stock OTA staging region, whose native overlap with LittleFS is deliberate and may erase the overlay; NET/RF/BLE-bonding metadata remains outside that write. Uses bk7231tools for probing, backup, aligned write/verify, and reboot.
  • Bouffalo: rebuilds the single application image and writes only the application FW slot; boot2, both partition-table copies, Safeboot, vendor regions, and LittleFS are neither rebuilt nor written, and the FW active index is preserved so a device in Safeboot stays there. Uses the pinned blflashcommand package with the loader's SHA-256 verification.
  • Pico: rebuilds the single application image and writes only the application slot at its XIP bus address after validating the installed Newmota table; its embedded copy of that table is rewritten with the image, while Safeboot, LittleFS, the marker, and the E10 reserve are untouched (marker preserved). Uses the pinned picotool CLI with per-component read-back verification; the board must be in BOOTSEL mode.

docs.title: ESP flash capacity
docs.text: ESP flashing probes the actual capacity. A device smaller than the package is rejected. For a larger device, Newmota regenerates a temporary partition table with ESP-IDF's official generator and grows only the final filesystem partition; fixed offsets and the package contents remain unchanged during flashing. Probe data and the exact write plan are retained under build/work/<environment>/flash/<size>/.

docs.title: Upgrade 1 transport
docs.text:
• Transport: Accepts direct HTTP 200 responses with an explicit Content-Length. HTTP redirects, chunked transfer encoding, and HTTPS are deliberately rejected.
  • Native Writers: Streams chunks directly to the alternate partition or OTA writer without buffering the image in RAM. Image slot sizes are validated before writing.
  • Progress Tracking: Querying Upgrade reports real-time transfer progress and final verification status.

docs.title: Parallel Build Acceleration
docs.text:
Native SDK adapters automatically pass parallel job flags (JOBS=N or make -j) to sub-builders that support concurrent compilation (such as CMake or Ninja).

If ccache is found in the host system's PATH, platform build adapters prepend ccache to compiler invocations automatically.

docs.title: SDK Logging (SDK_LOG_LEVEL)
docs.text:
Every native build uses the global SDK_LOG_LEVEL setting, resolved at build time and translated into each native SDK's configuration. It defaults to warn and accepts none, error, warn, info, debug, or verbose:

make build ENV=esp32c2-2m SDK_LOG_LEVEL=none

Newmota's own logging stays on its platform console, so none only removes SDK diagnostics — useful for flash-size measurements. Change the single Make variable default when the project policy changes; no alternate build target is required. (BL602, BL616, and BL618DG Safeboot images always use none to fit their recovery partitions. The Beken mapping is provisional: the CB2S test build shows no meaningful size reduction with none, so its SDK log elimination is not yet treated as proven.)

docs.title: Build lifecycle stages
docs.text:
Every firmware build executes an explicit, standardized 7-stage lifecycle managed by tools/newmota/pipeline.py.

graph LR
    S1[1. Resolve] --> S2[2. Prepare]
    S2 --> S3[3. Configure]
    S3 --> S4[4. Pre-Build]
    S4 --> S5[5. Build]
    S5 --> S6[6. Post-Build]
    S6 --> S7[7. Package]

docs.title: Stage 1: resolve
docs.text: Resolves target environment parameters from config/env/<platform>/<role>/, config/boards/, and config/chips/. Determines role (application or safeboot), chip family, physical flash capacity, console UART assignment, SDK path, and required toolchain versions. If an application declares a safeboot: companion, it resolves and queues the safeboot build first.

docs.title: Stage 2: prepare
docs.text: Verifies toolchain and SDK readiness. If toolchains or the SDK release archive are missing, lazy setup triggers automatically to download pinned tools without failing the build.

docs.title: Stage 3: configure
docs.text: Merges immutable chip SDK defaults (config/build/<platform>/<chip>/) with board configuration and environment profile parameters, generating target build files inside build/work/<environment>/config/.

docs.title: Stage 4: pre-build
docs.text: Prepares stage build directories, pre-compiles LittleFS partition binaries (filesystem.bin) using littlefs-python, and generates C++ header files containing firmware version metadata.

docs.title: Stage 5: build
docs.text: Invokes the native cross-compiler toolchain and native SDK build runner (CMake, Ninja, or Makefile). Compiles application code (src/app/) and platform bindings (src/platform/<platform>/) into object files and executable binaries.

docs.title: Stage 6: post-build
docs.text: Invokes platform-specific binary processors: - ESP-IDF: Generates application, bootloader, and partition table images via esptool. - Raspberry Pi Pico: Generates newmota.elf, newmota.bin, and drag-and-drop newmota.uf2 binaries, embedding the application-owned partition table at build time (ELF path). - Bouffalo: Runs bflb_fw_post_proc --ptfile against the Newmota-decided TOML for partition-aware application + Safeboot boot images. - Beken: Produces the native AXF/raw diagnostic image, the CRC-wrapped application RBL for wired flashing, and the compressed/encrypted RBL for single-image OTA staging. - AmebaD: Assembles dual-core KM0 and KM4 binaries into combined bootloader and application images.

docs.title: Stage 7: package
docs.text:
ESP-IDF builds create a checksummed development factory package; Bouffalo and Pico builds create paired factory packages plus wired application-only update paths; Beken builds create target-validated factory and stock-OTA artifacts; and the AmebaD bw16-2m build creates a paired factory package plus a wired OTA2 update path. ESP-IDF signed OTA and all other platform release/deployment paths remain untested.

For packaging platforms, an immutable development factory package is written under build/firmware/<environment>/<version>/ containing: - Merged factory flash images (ESP-IDF), paired Safeboot + application FW images with boot2/tables (Bouffalo) or marker-aware slots (Pico), RBL factory + stock-OTA artifacts (Beken), or the paired Safeboot + application image2 outputs, boot images, LittleFS image, and flashloader (AmebaD). - Offset-addressed individual component binaries. - Immutable package manifest.json recording build timestamps, board parameters, git revisions, tool versions, role metadata, and SHA-256 hashes of all binary outputs. Platforms without a packaging path fail closed rather than generating misleading packages.

One BuildDateTime value (YYYY.MM.DD HH:MM:SS) is generated per build invocation and shared by every image in that build — application and Safeboot companions carry the same stamp, embedded in PlatformInfo (surfaced as StatusFWR) and recorded in the manifest. The local build timezone is used by default; setting SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH produces a reproducible UTC timestamp instead.

Rebuilding an existing environment and version combination that results in different output bytes is treated as an explicit error to maintain build reproducibility and packaging integrity.

docs.title: Editor & clangd Setup
docs.text: Newmota provides target-aware clangd language server support to enable full C/C++ code completion, navigation, and static analysis in modern IDEs (VS Code, Neovim, CLion, Emacs).

docs.title: Why Target-Aware clangd?
docs.text:
Embedded multi-platform development involves different cross-compilers (xtensa-esp32-elf-gcc, riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc, arm-none-eabi-gcc), architecture macros, system header paths, and SDK headers. Merging compile commands across target platforms produces index corruption.

Newmota generates precise, single-environment compilation databases without host compiler fallbacks.

docs.title: Activating clangd for an Environment
docs.text:
Generate compile commands for an exact target environment:

make clangd ENV=esp32c2-2m

Or for a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W target:

make clangd ENV=pico2-w

Or for a RISC-V Bouffalo target:

make clangd ENV=bl602-2m

docs.title: What make clangd Does
docs.text:
1. Runs lazy toolchain setup and lifecycle stages: resolve → prepare → configure → pre-build.
  2. Queries the target platform's native build system for real compilation arguments.
  3. Filters entries to include project-owned C++ source code (src/app/, src/platform/).
  4. Generates a target-specific database at build/clangd/<environment>/compile_commands.json.
  5. Symlinks or copies the database to the repository root (compile_commands.json), activating it for clangd-compatible editors.

docs.title: Cross-Compiler Normalization
docs.text:
Raw cross-compiler flags often cause parsing errors in upstream clangd instances. Newmota's compilation database generator (tools/newmota/compdb.py) automatically performs normalization:

  • System Header Discovery: Queries the target cross-compiler directly for its internal system include directories (-isystem) and appends them to each compilation entry.
  • GCC Flag Stripping: Filters out target-specific GCC code-generation flags that clangd does not recognize.
  • Xtensa Architecture Markers: Injects Xtensa architecture definitions for ESP32/S2/S3 targets so clangd can parse ESP-IDF header files accurately.

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text: Newmota uses a dual-level environment strategy: Python tooling is managed locally with uv, while platform cross-compiler toolchains and native SDKs are maintained under user tool directories (~/.espressif and ~/.newmota/tools/).

docs.title: Python Environment (uv)
docs.text:
The project uses uv for fast, deterministic Python environment management.

# Create and synchronize .venv
make uv-setup

The pyproject.toml pins the host dependencies, including: - littlefs-python == 0.18.0: Host-side LittleFS filesystem image generation and manifest verification. - pyserial == 3.5: Wired serial communication and flashing adapters. - pyyaml >= 6.0: Catalog and environment configuration parsing. - blflashcommand (Git-pinned Staars/blflashcommand) and bflb-fw-post-proc == 1.4.5: Bouffalo flashing and image post-processing. - bk7231tools == 2.1.2: Beken probing, backup, and flashing. - brotli, zopfli: build-time web asset compression (Brotli for HTTPS builds, Gzip for HTTP builds).

The dev extra adds ruff (Python lint, settings in pyproject.toml) and the pinned clang-format used by make format-cpp. Use uv run --locked --extra dev ruff check tools to check the Python tooling.

docs.title: Toolchain & SDK Directories
docs.text:
Platform toolchains and SDK assets are kept separate from the repository source code and the Python .venv.

Platform Toolchain Location Environment Variables ESP-IDF ~/.espressif IDF_TOOLS_PATH Raspberry Pi ~/.newmota/tools/arm-none-eabi/ & ~/.newmota/tools/pico-sdk/ NEWMOTA_TOOLS_PATH Bouffalo Pinned native XuanTie release + ~/.newmota/tools/bouffalo/<version>/ NEWMOTA_TOOLS_PATH Beken ~/.newmota/tools/arm-none-eabi/ NEWMOTA_TOOLS_PATH AmebaD ~/.newmota/tools/amebad/<version>/ NEWMOTA_TOOLS_PATH

docs.title: Host Python Isolation
docs.text:
Native SDK installers (especially ESP-IDF) invoke a host Python interpreter outside Newmota's .venv. This design ensures that ESP-IDF's internal virtual environments (~/.espressif/python_env/) remain independent of Newmota's development environment.

To override the host Python interpreter if necessary:

make setup ENV=esp32c2-2m SDK_PYTHON=/usr/local/bin/python3

SDK installers need a host Python 3.10 or newer outside the project virtual environment.

docs.title: Apple Silicon Bouffalo note
docs.text: On Apple Silicon, Bouffalo setup downloads the pinned native Xuantie GCC 14 release with its host dependencies included; a separate Homebrew runtime-library install is not required. Bouffalo flashing uses the pinned blflashcommand Python package, so no Rosetta is needed.

docs.title: SDK Pinning & Release Archives
docs.text:
Every SDK is pinned to one commit of a Newmota fork. Builds download a stripped, checksummed release archive of that commit from Newmota/sdk-archives and extract it read-only into ~/.newmota/sdk/ (NEWMOTA_SDK_PATH moves it). No Git submodules are needed, and only the SDKs a build uses are downloaded.

  • ESP-IDF v5.5.5 from the Newmota/esp-idf fork, branch newmota/v5.5.5 (the tag plus the external Wi-Fi crypto that WPA3 on BearSSL needs), with esptool 4.14.0.
  • ESP-IDF v6.1 from the same fork, branch newmota/v6.1 (the tag plus the same change), with esptool 5.3.1. make setup PLATFORM=esp prepares both tracks.
  • Pico SDK v2.3.1 from Newmota/pico-sdk (the upstream release, unpatched).
  • BouffaloSDK v2.3.34 from Newmota/bouffalo_sdk.
  • Beken BDK v3.0.78 from Newmota/framework-beken-bdk.
  • Realtek AmebaD snapshot 2026-06-18-newmota.4 from Newmota/ameba-rtos-d.

make sdk-fetch downloads every archive in advance for offline builds. For SDK patch work, make sdk-checkout SDK=<key> clones the pinned commit into .sdk/<source> (ignored by Git); while that checkout exists, builds use it instead of the archive.

Human-readable SDK version declarations live under config/sdk/:

config/sdk/
├── esp-idf.toml
├── esp-idf-v6.1.toml
├── esp-idf-v5.5.constraints.txt
├── esp-idf-v6.1.constraints.txt
├── pico-sdk.toml
├── bouffalo.toml
├── beken.toml
└── amebad.toml

Before running builds, Newmota checks that the installed SDK matches its pin in config/sdk/<platform>.toml: the archive checksum and its recorded commit, or the commit of a .sdk/ checkout. Run make sdk-check at any time to verify every installed SDK.

docs.title: Compiler Acceleration (ccache)
docs.text:
If ccache is installed on your host system and available in PATH, Newmota's native platform build adapters automatically integrate it into cross-compiler invocations.

# Verify ccache availability
which ccache

No additional configuration is necessary; missing ccache falls back smoothly to normal compilation without failure.

docs.title: Source & Config Reference
docs.text: Reference for contributors: where firmware configuration lives, how the source tree is organized, and what a build produces. End users don't need this page — see First Steps and Daily Use instead.

docs.title: Configuration catalog (config/)
docs.text:
Newmota uses a declarative catalog model to define supported microcontrollers, target board recipes, firmware environments, SDK settings, and partition layouts.

The configuration hierarchy lives under config/, with local configurations in user_config/ and browser locales in language/:

config/
├── chips/        # Public chip declarations and capabilities
├── boards/       # Hardware recipes (chip, flash, PSRAM, console UART)
├── env/          # Firmware build policies and matrices
├── build/        # Immutable vendor SDK default configurations
├── hardware/     # Frozen GPIO function IDs, pin topologies, product modules, display descriptors
├── sdk/          # SDK & host-programmer version pins, plus ESP-IDF Python constraints
└── partitions/   # Native partition layouts keyed by flash size

user_config/      # Ignored personal environments (inherit: <base-id>)
language/         # Build-time browser locale catalogs (en_GB.toml, de_DE.toml)

docs.title: 1. Chip Catalog (config/chips/<platform>/)
docs.text: Maps a public chip identifier (e.g. esp32c2, rp2350, bl602, bk7231n, rtl8720dn) to its native SDK target, processor architecture, flash interfaces, and baseline capabilities.

docs.title: 2. Board Recipes (config/boards/<platform>/)
docs.text: Defines native physical hardware recipes (e.g. pico2-w.json, esp32s3-qio-qspi.json). A board recipe specifies: - chip: The target chip identifier. - flash: Physical flash memory capacity (size_kb), bus mode (qio, dio), and speed (frequency_mhz). - psram: Optional PSRAM memory size, bus mode, and clock frequency. - console: Active console peripheral (uart0, usb-cdc, or usb-serial-jtag). - profile_default: Assigned resource profile baseline (Compact, Standard, Large, Safeboot).

docs.title: 3. Environment Specifications & Explicit Roles (config/env/<platform>/<role>/)
docs.text:
Defines complete, buildable firmware environment targets. Environments are partitioned into explicit role directories:

  • application/: Primary application firmware images.
  • safeboot/: Minimal recovery firmware images built to perform emergency recovery or staging.
# config/env/esp-idf/application/esp32s3-qio-qspi.yaml
name: esp32s3-qio-qspi
board: esp32s3-qio-qspi
role: application
profile: Standard
safeboot: esp32s3-qio-qspi-safeboot
language: en_GB

Applications can explicitly declare their paired safeboot dependency (safeboot: <env>). When an application specifies a safeboot companion, the build pipeline automatically builds and packages the safeboot image before packaging the application. Current pairs: esp32s3-qio-qspi → esp32s3-qio-qspi-safeboot, bw16-2m → bw16-2m-safeboot, bl602-2m → bl602-2m-safeboot, pico2-w → pico2-w-safeboot, pico-w → pico-w-safeboot. Beken has no safeboot environments by design; cb2s-2m, cb3s (BK7231N), and xh-cb3s (BK7238) are application-only.

config/env/matrices/
└── test.txt     # Routine cross-platform test matrix (4 Compact + 1 Standard target)

docs.title: 4. Immutable SDK Defaults (config/build/<platform>/<chip>/)
docs.text:
Contains native vendor SDK default settings: - ESP-IDF: sdkconfig.defaults (and platform-common settings in common/sdkconfig.defaults). - Pico SDK: Native cmake.defaults definitions. - Bouffalo / Beken / AmebaD: Native defconfig files.

During a build, Newmota merges these defaults with board requirements and environment flags into build/work/<environment>/config/. Checked-in defaults and the SDK sources are never modified.

docs.title: 5. SDK & Toolchain Version Pins (config/sdk/)
docs.text: Stores human-readable version declarations for SDKs and host tools (esp-idf.toml, esp-idf-v6.1.toml, pico-sdk.toml, bouffalo.toml, beken.toml, amebad.toml). These files declare: - Upstream release label and exact Git commit hash. - Toolchain releases and download URLs. - External tool archive SHA-256 checksums.

docs.title: 6. Partition Definitions (config/partitions/<platform>/)
docs.text:
Contains partition tables keyed by total physical flash capacity: esp-idf/{2,4,8,16}m.csv (exact Tasmota schemes), bouffalo/2m.toml (BL602 asymmetric FW slots + dedicated LittleFS) and bouffalo/4m-{bl602,bl616,bl618dg}.toml (target-specific application/Safeboot slots + LittleFS), beken/{2m,2m-bk7238,4m}.toml (native OTA envelope with LittleFS tail overlay), amebad/2m.toml, pico-sdk/4m-rp2350.json (official picotool JSON for RP2350), and pico-sdk/2m-rp2040.json (project-owned checked layout for RP2040). Immutable native SDK defaults live in config/build/<platform>/<chip>/; each build resolves those defaults with its board and environment settings into build/work/<environment>/config/ without modifying the SDK checkout. Board and chip files never contain partition or filesystem allocation fields. Beken has no Safeboot or alternate-image layout by design.

Partition and native-configuration choices follow the porting reference hierarchy: an existing Newmota implementation is preferred, otherwise the ESP-IDF/Tasmota configuration for the matching flash class is the default starting baseline where no stronger platform-specific reference exists. Native SDK boot constraints, image formats, alignment, reserved regions, and hardware evidence may require a deliberate deviation, which is recorded with the resulting layout.

docs.title: Catalog Validation (make validate-catalog)
docs.text:
Newmota includes a catalog validation step (tools/newmota/catalog.py) that checks the consistency of all JSON/YAML configuration files without invoking compilers or downloading SDKs.

make validate-catalog

Validation checks include: - Cross-references between chips, board recipes, and environment files. - Consistency of partition table total flash allocations. - Integrity of SDK pin declarations against expected structure. - Compatibility of target-specific memory and console UART choices.

docs.title: Source tree (src/)
docs.text:
The Newmota repository layout separates portable application code, platform adapters, build tools, configuration files, and upstream vendor SDK checkouts. Portable code lives in src/app/; platform implementations and their native SDK integration live together under src/platform/ behind a small public contract. There is no host compiler fallback — every build compiles through a platform's native SDK.

docs.title: Build tooling (tools/newmota/)
docs.text:
make is the public interface; it forwards commands to PYTHONPATH=tools python -m newmota (unified CLI in __main__.py with lazy dispatch). Ownership rules live in the build-tool ownership guide, tools/README.md in the Newmota repository: shared orchestration selects a platform through the platforms registry and never imports a platform implementation directly; a platform may import shared modules and its own helpers, but never another platform.

tools/newmota/
├── __main__.py         # Unified CLI: argument parsing + lazy command dispatch
├── catalog.py          # Catalog parsing, board schema, validation orchestration
├── config.py           # Native config layering and identity (sdkconfig/defconfig/cmake)
├── pipeline.py         # Selection, dependency ordering, lifecycle, native manifest
├── package.py          # Manifest safety, layout facts, empty LittleFS images
├── device.py           # Device contract, port selection, device workflows
├── host.py             # Processes, SDK pins, toolchains, common staging helpers
├── features.py         # Common feature policy, dependencies, source ownership
├── berry.py            # Berry generation and incremental inputs
├── web.py              # Deterministic Gzip/Brotli embedding of the web UI asset
├── i18n.py             # Locale catalog validation and rendering
├── ota.py / audio.py / crypto.py / lvgl.py / energy_inventory.py # Feature-specific build helpers
├── compdb.py           # Compilation database collection and activation
├── hardware.py / topology.py # Hardware catalog + topology resolution helpers
└── platforms/          # One explicit, lazy platform registry (__init__.py)
    ├── esp/            # Public selector esp; native SDK dir esp-idf
    │   ├── build.py    # Setup, requirements/target checks, build adapter
    │   ├── images.py   # Layout resolution, image checks, packaging, Safeboot checks
    │   ├── device.py   # Programmer protocol, write bounds, verification, monitoring
    │   └── usb_monitor.py # USB-safe no-reset serial monitor launcher
    ├── bouffalo/       # build.py / images.py / device.py (blflashcommand path)
    ├── beken/          # build.py / images.py / device.py + specialists:
    │                   # bdk.py, codec.py, profile.py (profile shared, dependency-free)
    ├── amebad/         # build.py / images.py / device.py + uploader.py
    └── pico/           # Public selector pico; native SDK dir pico-sdk
                        # build.py / images.py / device.py (picotool path)

docs.title: Build outputs (build/)
docs.text:
Build artifacts are generated under build/ and ignored by version control:

build/
├── clangd/             # Generated per-environment compile_commands.json
├── firmware/           # Packaged development factory images & manifests
│   └── <environment>/
│       └── <version>/
│           ├── manifest.json   # Immutable manifest: timestamps, board params,
│           │                   # git revisions, tool versions, roles, SHA-256 hashes
│           ├── factory.bin     # (ESP-IDF) combined factory flash image
│           └── filesystem.bin  # Pre-generated LittleFS partition image
└── work/               # Staged SDK build dirs, native objects, checkummed manifest
    └── <environment>/
        ├── config/     # Resolved native SDK build configs
        └── flash/<size>/ # Probe data + exact write plan for larger flash chips

Native SDK work and its checksummed build manifest live under build/work/<environment>/ — these are not automatically deployable firmware. All five platform packagers (ESP-IDF, Bouffalo, Beken, AmebaD, Pico SDK) write their manifest, factory components, layout source, and debug files under build/firmware/<environment>/<version>/ and never mislabel the application binary as OTA firmware. Rebuilding the same environment/version replaces the generated package; rebuilding with different output bytes is an explicit error.

docs.title: Personal Build Configurations
docs.text:
Newmota allows developers and power users to define custom, local build environments without modifying checked-in repository files. Personal configurations live under user_config/ and are ignored by git.

Tip

make config writes this file for you from a menu; see Build Your Firmware. This page covers editing it by hand, including the fields the menu does not set (crypto, idf_version, native, solidify, filesystem). The menu keeps these fields when it reopens the file.

docs.title: Defining a Personal Configuration
docs.text:
Create a YAML file in user_config/<custom-id>.yaml that inherits from any checked-in application environment:

# user_config/my-c2-plug.yaml
name: my-c2-plug
inherit: esp32c2-2m
language: de_DE
crypto: none

Another example enabling the full crypto test suite on an ESP32-S3:

# user_config/s3-crypto-full.yaml
name: s3-crypto-full
inherit: esp32s3-qio-opi
profile: Standard
crypto: all

docs.title: Allowed Overrides
docs.text:
To maintain layout integrity and device safety, personal configurations can only override specific explicit fields:

Field Description Values / Examples inherit Required. The checked-in base application environment ID. esp32c2-2m, esp32s3-qio-qspi, pico2-w, pico-w, cb2s-2m, etc. profile Firmware resource profile budget. Compact, Standard, Large language Build-time browser locale catalog (one per firmware, no runtime switch). en_GB, de_DE (from language/); en is an alias for en_GB features Optional compiled driver features (merges by key). Map of booleans such as USE_BME280, USE_BH1750, USE_TC74, USE_DHT, USE_I2C, USE_WS2812, USE_I2S, USE_DISPLAY, USE_DISPLAY_QSPI, USE_UNIVERSAL_TOUCH, USE_LVGL, USE_WEB_HTTPS, USE_BLE, USE_BLE_SENSORS, USE_MATTER, USE_GPS, RTC chips, and the energy drivers. See below. crypto BearSSL and Berry crypto feature selection. all, none, or a mapping with berry and primitives idf_version Pinned ESP-IDF SDK track (ESP targets only). "5.5" (default) or "6.1" native Platform-specific native SDK build flags or overrides. Map of vendor-specific SDK key-values solidify Berry driver classes built into flash instead of uploaded. List of driver files, such as berry/drivers/camera/ov2640.be. See below. filesystem Files written into the factory filesystem image. List of file paths, or mappings with source and target. See below.

Immutable Base Properties

Chip architecture, target board recipe, partition layout, Safeboot companion pairing, and role are inherited directly from the checked-in base environment and cannot be overridden. This ensures that flashing offsets, memory maps, and bootloader requirements remain valid.

docs.title: Built-in Berry Drivers
docs.text:
solidify lists Berry driver files whose classes the build puts into flash, so no upload is needed and the classes take no heap. Only the classes a file marks with #@ solidify:<Class> are built in; nothing runs at startup. autoexec.be still creates and registers them, which lets one firmware carry competing drivers and each board pick its own:

name: eye-cam
inherit: esp32s3-qio-opi-8m-8m
features:
  USE_WEBCAM: true
solidify:
  - berry/drivers/camera/ov2640.be

# autoexec.be
cam.register(OV2640())

Paths are relative to the firmware repository; files of your own can live in user_config/. List every file a class needs, bases first: segment_display.be before tm1637.be. The build refuses a file whose #@ requires: features are off, a class whose base is missing or listed later, and code other than classes at a file's top level. A file loaded at runtime replaces a built-in class of the same name, so a fixed driver can be tried without a rebuild.

docs.title: Files in the Factory Filesystem
docs.text:
filesystem lists files the build writes into the factory LittleFS image. A path lands at /<file name>; a mapping with source and target puts it elsewhere or renames it:

filesystem:
  - berry/drivers/camera/ov2640.be            # lands at /ov2640.be
  - source: berry/drivers/camera/isp/ov5647.json
    target: /isp.json
  - source: user_config/eye-cam-autoexec.be
    target: /autoexec.be

Note

Only a factory flash writes these files; OTA updates and Safeboot never touch the filesystem. They are defaults: after the first boot they belong to you and may be edited or deleted.

The build refuses a file that is also in solidify, two entries with one target, targets inside /.newmota or /sd, .be files whose #@ requires: features are off, and files that do not fit the factory filesystem. solidify and filesystem append to the inherited lists.

docs.title: Optional Features
docs.text:
Select optional modules with a boolean features mapping. Dependencies are selected automatically; setting a dependency to false while selecting a feature that needs it is an error, as are unknown names and features that the platform, role, or flash size does not support. Optional features are application-only (the paired Safeboot keeps its own selection), and the resolved selection is written to build/work/<environment>/config/feature_map.json.

name: workshop-c2
inherit: esp32c2-2m
features:
  USE_BH1750: true
  USE_TC74: true
Feature Default Notes USE_I2C, I2C sensors (USE_BH1750, USE_TC74, USE_BME280), USE_DHT Off Sensors USE_BLE, USE_BLE_SENSORS Off Bluetooth & BLE Sensors; ESP-IDF, Bouffalo, AmebaD and Pico only. No checked-in profile selects them USE_MATTER, USE_MATTER_BLE, USE_MATTER_BRIDGE Off Matter; ESP-IDF and RP2350 with at least 4 MiB flash, or Beken (2 MiB, without MQTT; USE_MATTER_BLE and USE_MATTER_BRIDGE are ESP-IDF and RP2350 only). No checked-in profile selects them USE_GPS Off Optional GPS; UBX only, all families except BL616/BL618DG RTC chips (USE_DS3231, USE_DS1307, USE_BM8563, USE_PCF85063, USE_PCF85363, USE_RV3028, USE_RX8010, USE_RX8025, USE_RX8130) Off Optional RTC Chips USE_HA_DISCOVERY Off Home Assistant discovery; selects USE_MQTT. Enabled in the test environments while it is measured USE_NTP_SERVER Off Optional NTP Server Energy drivers (USE_PZEM004T, USE_MODBUS_ENERGY, …) Off Energy Metering USE_I2S, USE_AUDIO_MP3, USE_AUDIO_AAC, USE_AUDIO_OPUS Off At least 4 MiB flash; not on Beken or BL602 USE_DISPLAY, USE_UNIVERSAL_TOUCH, USE_DISPLAY_QSPI, USE_LVGL Off Displays & Touch; QSPI on ESP-IDF, BL616/BL618DG, and Pico only USE_WS2812 Off Not on Beken USE_WEB_HTTPS On for Large Off for Compact, Standard, and Safeboot USE_WIFI_WPA3_BEARSSL On for ESP chips with their own radio and at least 4 MiB flash (ESP-IDF 5.5 and 6.1), for BK7231N, BK7238 and BK7252N, and for Bouffalo BL602, BL616 and BL618DG Wi-Fi supplicant on BearSSL instead of mbedTLS, application and Safeboot. Not on ESP-Hosted chips (P4, P4X), whose companion runs the supplicant. With it off, C5, C6 and C61 Safeboot drop WPA3 to fit their slot. On Beken the prebuilt supplicant then runs on BearSSL, SAE with group 19 only, and images without HTTPS link no mbedTLS (about 22.9 KB smaller); BK7231T and BK7252, whose supplicant brings its own wolfSSL crypto, reject it. On Bouffalo, BL616 and BL618DG run the Wi-Fi 6 supplicant on BearSSL (SAE group 19 only); BL602 moves only the supplicant's hashes and keeps SAE on the SDK's blcrypto_suite. Bouffalo images without HTTPS then link no mbedTLS (application 20.8 KB smaller on BL616, 16.4 KB on BL602) USE_CRYPTO_HW_SHA1, USE_CRYPTO_HW_SHA256, USE_CRYPTO_HW_P256 On with USE_WIFI_WPA3_BEARSSL, where the chip has the engine BearSSL on the ESP and Bouffalo hardware engines; on Bouffalo, USE_CRYPTO_HW_SHA1 also derives the Wi-Fi PSK on the SHA engine. ESP32 has no usable SHA engine; ESP32-C2 has no P-256 engine USE_SERIAL, USE_DEVICE_SPI, USE_ADC, USE_MODBUS_RTU Off Shared hardware owners, selected automatically by drivers that need them

The complete list, with dependencies and platform limits, is OPTIONAL_FEATURES in tools/newmota/features.py in the firmware repository.

docs.title: Crypto defaults
docs.text: crypto is a compile-time choice that does not affect HTTPS. When omitted, ESP Standard and Large applications include the Matter crypto APIs plus SHA256, AES_GCM, MD5, and random; other applications include SHA256, MD5, and random; Safeboot includes none. A build that requests random fails if the platform has no entropy source.

docs.title: Mutable Settings Belong on the Device
docs.text:
Build-time configuration is reserved for compile-time properties (such as crypto algorithms or language packs). Do not attempt to embed Wi-Fi credentials or hardware pinouts in YAML files:

  • Wi-Fi, MQTT, DeviceName, OtaUrl: Configure via serial console commands or the device-hosted Web UI.
  • GPIO / Module / Template: Configure using Module, Template, or GPIO commands.

docs.title: Building Personal Environments
docs.text:
Personal environments integrate seamlessly into the make workflow:

# Check catalog and view personal environments
make list

# Validate personal configs alongside repository catalog
make validate-catalog

# Build the personal environment
make my-c2-plug

# Or using explicit ENV syntax
make build ENV=my-c2-plug

# Flash to device
make flash ENV=my-c2-plug

make all and the automated test matrix (make test) deliberately build only checked-in catalog environments, keeping personal builds strictly local.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: Newmota can play and record audio through I2S, control sessions from Berry, and configure supported external codecs and amplifiers. Audio is optional, excluded from standard builds, and still awaiting hardware qualification. It needs at least 4 MiB of flash. Beken support is deferred; BL602 has no I2S peripheral, and BL616/BL618DG do not yet have a Newmota I2S adapter. Available pins and modes depend on the chip.

docs.title: Enable audio
docs.text:
Choose features in make config or in a personal build by hand, selecting only the codecs you need:

name: audio-s3
inherit: esp32s3-qio-qspi
features:
  USE_I2S: true
  USE_AUDIO_MP3: true
  USE_AUDIO_AAC: true
  USE_AUDIO_OPUS: true
  USE_WEB_AUDIO: true

USE_I2S enables the transport and commands; USE_BERRY_AUDIO adds the Berry audio module. MP3 and Opus support playback and recording; AAC supports ADTS playback only. USE_AUDIO_SAM adds speech. The Berry module brings a microphone level meter, a spectrum analyzer and a tone generator (RTTTL on I2S). USE_WEB_AUDIO requires the web interface and adds a Home player when an I2S output is configured. Files stream through the filesystem rather than being loaded entirely into RAM; PCM and WAV files are not supported.

docs.title: Configure I2S
docs.text:
Assign the I2S GPIO functions in the device template. Standard output uses BCLK, WS and DOUT; an input uses DIN as well as its clocks. Some external codecs also need MCLK. Input (Rx) and output (Tx) have separate profiles, initially in standard mode. Select PDM explicitly for a PDM microphone; supported modes and pin routes depend on the chip. Pico and AmebaD do not support PDM.

Use I2SConfig to inspect or save profiles, with the command operation stopped:

I2SConfig
I2SConfig Rx.rate 16000
I2SConfig {"Rx":{"mode":"pdm","rate":16000,"slot_mask":1}}
I2SConfig reset

Profiles include rate, bits, slot width, framing and gain. Settings are checked against the device before saving, and are retained across restarts. I2SGain adjusts live playback volume; saving I2SConfig also stores the live gains. Reset restores template-derived defaults. Pins come from the template, not the saved profile. See the firmware repository's src/app/drivers/audio/README.md for platform-specific options and supported formats.

docs.title: Play and record
docs.text:
Commands share a session across the console, web, MQTT and Berry command interface. They cannot take over an active Berry audio session. For example, I2SPlay1 /chime.mp3 plays an MP3, I2SLoop1 /chime.mp3 repeats it, and I2SRec1 /recording.mp3 records MP3. Stop recording with I2SRec so it can finalize; I2SStop stops the command session. I2SPause pauses file playback, and a bare I2SPlay or I2SLoop resumes it.

Playback selectors are 0 for AAC, 1 for MP3 and 2 for Opus; an omitted selector is 0. Recording uses 1 for MP3 or 2 for Opus and defaults to 1. The selected codec must be compiled in. I2SWrN plays a plaintext HTTP/ICY stream; HTTPS and redirects are not supported. I2SStream 1 starts the microphone HTTP listener on port 81. See audio commands for the command list.

docs.title: Berry audio sessions
docs.text:
Berry controls native sessions through audio.Session. Configure the board's output pins first, then for example:

import audio
s = audio.Session({
  'source': 'file', 'sink': 'output', 'codec': 'mp3',
  'location': '/announcement.mp3', 'loop': false
})
s.start()
s.status()

Input and output maps start with the saved Rx and Tx profiles and can override settings and pins for a session. Recording uses source: 'microphone', sink: 'file', an enabled encoder and a file location. Hardware and pin ownership are shared, so conflicting sessions report Busy.

Call s.stop() and poll s.status() until state 2 (ended) before s.close(). Closing immediately can abort a recording before its final data is written. A completed session retains its hardware lease until closed; it can instead be reconfigured for another operation once ended. Status state 0 is closed, 1 running and 3 failed.

With the respective features enabled, audio.level and audio.spectrum analyze microphone input using the Rx profile. They are singletons and compete for the input; stop one before starting the other. Level readings are dBFS unless calibrated with audio.level.offset(). Spectrum results are available through audio.spectrum.bands().

docs.title: Board audio codecs and amplifiers
docs.text:
Berry drivers in berry/drivers/audio/ configure external audio chips over I2C. They require USE_I2C and USE_I2S; ES8311, PCM5122 and TAS58xx also require USE_BERRY_GPIO. The drivers can be uploaded and loaded at startup or included with a personal build's solidify list.

Driver Hardware es8311.be Mono DAC and microphone ADC, with optional amplifier enable es7210.be Four-channel microphone ADC es8388.be Stereo DAC and ADC es8156.be Stereo DAC es7243e.be Stereo microphone ADC pcm5122.be Stereo DAC, with optional soft-mute pin tas58xx.be TAS5805M and TAS5825M Class-D amplifiers, with optional power-down pin

For example, configure the board's I2C and I2S pins and enable USE_BERRY_DRIVERS, then load and register an ES8311 in /autoexec.be:

load("es8311.be")  # omit when solidified
codec = ES8311(53)  # replace 53 with the board's amplifier-enable GPIO, or nil
newmota.add_driver(codec)

Registration lets the ES8311 follow output power and stream rate. The ES7210 follows input rate; the PCM5122 and TAS58xx follow output power. The audio hook runs on the next Berry poll, so an amplifier may miss the first milliseconds of a stream. The ES8311, ES7210, ES8388 and ES7243E require I2S MCLK at 256 times the sample rate (384 times for 24-bit ES8311); PCM5122 derives its clock from BCLK. Check each driver's header and the firmware audio README for supported formats, pin wiring and controls. The TAS58xx keeps its output off after DC or over-current faults until activate() is called.

docs.title: Berry Scripting
docs.text:
Berry is Newmota's tiny automation language: one-liners on the console (Br) and a startup script (/autoexec.be) that runs at every boot. It works in every normal build, including small 2 MiB devices — only the minimal Safeboot recovery image leaves it out.

Note

Berry here is the same language Tasmota uses, so Tasmota Berry examples largely apply. What Berry can reach (commands, hardware) is still growing — when in doubt, the console command it wraps is the same one you'd type yourself.

docs.title: Where Berry runs
docs.text: Berry is compiled into every normal application build on every chip family (2 MiB Compact included) and left out only of Safeboot recovery images, which have no room for a scripting engine.

docs.title: Interactive Command (Berry / Br)
docs.text:
The console processor exposes the Br (or Berry) command to evaluate expressions and run statements:

> Br 1 + 2
{"Br":"3"}

> Br for i: 0..3 print(i) end
{"Br":"nil"}

docs.title: Safety & Execution Deadlines
docs.text:
To prevent runaway scripts or infinite loops from hanging the microcontroller:

  1. Heartbeat Watchdog Hook: The VM installs an execution observer (BE_OBS_VM_HEARTBEAT) that monitors CPU run time.
  2. 4-Second Execution Deadline: Any single script execution exceeding 4000 ms is automatically interrupted, raising an exception: 
    {"Br":"timeout_error: Berry code running for too long"}
  3. Protected Calls (pcall): Script evaluation and result string conversion are executed within a protected context. Exceptions leave the Berry VM clean without leaking allocated stack frames.

docs.title: Log Routing & Logging
docs.text:
Berry's built-in print() function is connected directly to Newmota's central logging facility, routing script output to serial consoles and Web/Berry console histories. In addition, Tasmota-compatible log(message, level) writes directly to log sinks at the specified log level:

print("Hello from Berry on Newmota!")
log("Warning condition detected", 2)

The device keeps the last 8 lines of Berry output for the console. A console error report takes at most 7 of them — the error message first, then the traceback — and ends with (traceback truncated, full trace in the log) when it is longer, so a long traceback never hides its error. The log keeps every line.

docs.title: newmota — Commands, Timers, Cron & Utilities
docs.text:
Newmota exposes the global newmota object (matching Tasmota's tasmota object pattern) with built-in methods for commands, scheduling, and system info:

# Run a command and inspect structured results
var result = newmota.cmd("Power1 on")
print("Relay state:", result["POWER1"])

# Run a quiet command
var net = newmota.cmd("_Status 5")
print("IP:", net["StatusNET"]["IPAddress"])

# Run command chains
var multi = newmota.cmd("Power1 on; Dimmer 50")

# Millisecond timers and scheduling
var now = newmota.millis()
if newmota.time_reached(now + 1000)
  print("One second passed")
end

# Non-blocking timers (shares 16 callback slots with cron and defer)
newmota.set_timer(2000, def () print("Fired after 2 seconds") end, "my_timer")
newmota.remove_timer("my_timer")

# Cooperative delay and execution yield
newmota.delay(10)  # Sleep 0..50 ms cooperatively
newmota.yield()    # Yield to RTOS / network tasks

# Time, formatting & cron
var epoch = newmota.rtc()
var time_dict = newmota.time_dump(epoch)
var formatted = newmota.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", epoch)

# Local-time cron recurrence (six fields: sec min hour day-of-month month day-of-week)
newmota.add_cron("0 */15 * * * *", def () print("Quarter-hour tick") end, "cron_15m")
newmota.remove_cron("cron_15m")

# Wi-Fi status
var wifi = newmota.wifi()
print("Wi-Fi Quality:", wifi["quality"], "IP:", wifi["ip"])

# Trigger manual garbage collection
newmota.gc()

docs.title: light — Hardware Light Control & Gamma
docs.text:
When Light support is compiled and configured (SetOption15 1), Berry exposes the global light object for owner-backed control:

# Read state of Light endpoint 0
var st = light.get(0)
print("Power:", st["power"], "Applied:", st["applied_power"])
print("Brightness:", st["bri"], "Color Temperature:", st["ct"])

# Synchronous state update
light.set(0, {"power": true, "bri": 75, "ct": 320})

# Set RGB color
light.set(0, {"rgb": [255, 0, 128]})

# Pure-integer gamma helpers
var g10 = light.gamma10(512)
var g8 = light.gamma8(128)

docs.title: Pixel Framebuffers (pixmat)
docs.text: The global pixmat class provides high-speed native framebuffers for 2D matrices and strip layouts independently of display or strip hardware: - Formats: 1 byte (grayscale), 2 bytes (packed), 3 bytes (RGB 0xRRGGBB), or 4 bytes (RGBW 0xRRGGBBWW). - Constructors: pixmat(width, height, bpp[, serpentine]), pixmat(bytes_buf, width, height, bpp), or pixmat(bitplane, bytes_per_line). - Methods: get(x, y), set(x, y, color[, bri]), clear([byte]), blit(source, dx, dy), blit(packed_glyph_bits, ...), scroll(direction), buffer(), deinit().

docs.title: WS2812 LED Strips (led_strip)
docs.text:
Construct standalone addressable strips or borrow the configured Light strip: 

s = led_strip(4, 30, "GRB")
s.set(0, 0x00FF00)  # Green
s.show()
s.close()

docs.title: Display Controller (display())
docs.text: When compiled with USE_DISPLAY: true, Berry exposes the global display() class bound to the panel defined in /display.ini: - Methods: width(), height(), pixel(x, y, color), fill_rect(x, y, w, h, color), refresh(), power(on), invert(on), rotation(0..3), brightness(0..255).

docs.title: Audio sessions
docs.text: With USE_I2S, Berry can play, record and analyze audio through import audio and audio.Session. See Audio for setup and session lifecycle.

docs.title: Berry drivers and commands
docs.text:
With the default-off USE_BERRY_DRIVERS feature, Berry scripts do the jobs of Tasmota Rules the way Tasmota's Berry drivers and commands do. newmota.add_driver(obj) registers any instance, without a limit; newmota.remove_driver(obj) removes it. For each event Newmota looks up the method name on every driver, in registration order, as Tasmota does: a class method or any member that holds a function, also one assigned after add_driver(). It calls the function as f(obj, cmd, idx, payload, raw) with raw nil; cmd and payload are empty strings except for audio. Berry ignores unused arguments. Adding a driver twice does nothing. The global Driver class is Tasmota's: an instance with one variable per hook, so d = Driver(), d.every_second = def (self) ... end and newmota.add_driver(d) work in any order.

Method When idx every_50ms, every_100ms, every_250ms, every_second Scheduler ticks 0 any_key Each button or switch key, as Tasmota's SendKey device_save<<24 \| key<<16 \| state<<8 \| device, key 0 button, 1 switch, state Tasmota's POWER_* code switch_action Newmota extension: each detached SetOption114 switch Action, which Tasmota shows only to Rules Same packing as any_key, key 1 button_pressed Debounced press or release count<<24 \| level<<16 \| last_level<<8 \| index, level 0 pressed, zero-based index button_multi_pressed Completed one to five presses; not a SetOption13 immediate press count<<8 \| index set_power_handler Each Power command, interlock step or group write, changed or not, as Tasmota's SetDevicePower Bit mask of all Power states after it, bit 0 Power1 network_up, network_down Station or Ethernet address gained or lost 0 audio With USE_I2S: an I2S direction starts, changes its rate or stops. cmd "rate" comes first on a start or rate change, then "power"; payload is "tx" or "rx" The sample rate for rate; 1 on start, 0 on stop for power

As in Tasmota, a method that returns true ends that event's dispatch: the drivers after it do not see it. A driver removed during dispatch shifts the later ones, so the next one misses that event, also as in Tasmota. Unlike Tasmota, the hooks only observe: native button, switch and Power actions always happen. Detach inputs with SetOption73 1 (buttons) or SetOption114 1 (switches) to handle them in Berry alone. Hooks run in the Berry poll after the event, never inside it, so a command a hook issues produces its own events in a later poll. A Light change without a Power command, such as Dimmer 0, also calls set_power_handler once the Power mask changes. Up to 40 input and Power events wait for the poll, enough for Power0 on 32 outputs; more are dropped with a log warning. Unlike Tasmota, a tick method (every_50ms to every_second) assigned after add_driver() starts within a second, so drivers without tick methods do not run the Berry poll on every tick. An exception in one driver is logged and does not stop the others. A hook that runs into the 4 s Berry deadline is aborted and ends the poll; the drivers after it miss that event. Sensor values, schedules and MQTT topics use the existing APIs; there is no Rules engine and no trigger syntax.

newmota.add_cmd(name, f) adds a command, as Tasmota's tasmota.add_cmd(). It runs only when no native command has the name, from any source (console, web, MQTT, newmota.cmd()), and matches the name without regard to case and without a trailing index. Newmota calls f(name, idx, payload, payload_json) with the name as registered, the index (1 without one), the payload string (empty without one) and json.load(payload), nil when it is not JSON. f must be a function or closure; a method raises, as in Tasmota. Adding a name again replaces its function; newmota.remove_cmd(name) removes the exact name. The function answers with one of newmota.resp_cmnd_done(), resp_cmnd_error(), resp_cmnd_failed() ({"<Name>":"Done"}, "Error", "Failed"), resp_cmnd_str(text) ({"<Name>":"<text>"}) or resp_cmnd(json) (the JSON as given); the last call wins. Without one the command answers nothing. A command that raises is logged and still answers with what it set before. A response longer than 1024 bytes fails the command. Driver.add_cmd(name, f) registers f(self, name, idx, payload, payload_json) for that driver.

class Follow
  # Power2 follows Power1.
  def set_power_handler(cmd, idx)
    var want = (idx & 1) != 0
    if want != ((idx & 2) != 0)
      newmota.cmd(want ? "Power2 ON" : "Power2 OFF")
    end
  end
  # With SetOption114 1, Switch1 toggles Power3 (state 2 is TOGGLE).
  def switch_action(cmd, idx)
    if (idx & 0xFF) == 1 && ((idx >> 8) & 0xFF) == 2
      newmota.cmd("Power3 TOGGLE")
    end
  end
end
newmota.add_driver(Follow())

var d = Driver()
d.every_second = def (self) log("tick") end
d.add_cmd("Greet", def (self, cmd, idx, payload) newmota.resp_cmnd_str("Hello " + payload) end)
newmota.add_driver(d)
# Greet World  ->  {"Greet":"Hello World"}

newmota.read_sensors() returns the MQTT SENSOR document as a string, as Tasmota's tasmota.read_sensors() does, for json.load(). It holds the switch states, sensors and energy fields with StatusSNS units and precision, without Tasmota's Time. It returns nil when there is nothing to report or the document exceeds the 1024-byte MQTT payload. Tasmota's optional display argument is accepted and ignored. A thermostat with hysteresis:

import json
class Thermostat
  var target, band, heating
  def init() self.target = 21.0 self.band = 0.5 self.heating = nil end
  def every_second()
    var raw = newmota.read_sensors()
    var s = raw != nil ? json.load(raw) : nil
    var t = s != nil && s.find("DS18B20") != nil ? s["DS18B20"].find("Temperature") : nil
    if t == nil return end
    var heat = self.heating
    if t < self.target - self.band heat = true end
    if t > self.target + self.band heat = false end
    if heat != nil && heat != self.heating     # switch only on a change
      self.heating = heat
      newmota.cmd(heat ? "Power1 ON" : "Power1 OFF")
    end
  end
end
newmota.add_driver(Thermostat())

docs.title: Digital GPIO (import gpio)
docs.text:
Directly read and control unassigned digital GPIO pins, or inspect configured functions: 

import gpio

# Check configured function assignments (e.g. Relays)
var pin = gpio.pin(gpio.REL1)
var used = gpio.pin_used(gpio.REL1)

# Configure unassigned pin as digital output
gpio.pin_mode(12, gpio.OUTPUT)
gpio.digital_write(12, gpio.HIGH)

# Read digital input level
gpio.pin_mode(14, gpio.PULLUP)
var level = gpio.digital_read(14)

# PWM on an unassigned pin or the template's Buzzer pin: 440 Hz at 50% duty (0..1023)
var buzzer = gpio.pin(gpio.BUZZER)
gpio.set_pwm_freq(buzzer, 440)
gpio.set_pwm(buzzer, 512)

set_pwm and set_pwm_freq follow Tasmota; a PWM phase is not supported. The firmware's examples/audio/rtttl.be plays RTTTL ringtones on a buzzer, or with Rtttl("i2s") on the I2S output (USE_BERRY_AUDIO), with the command Rtttl <song>.

docs.title: Hardware Serial Ports (import serial)
docs.text:
Access native hardware UART ports with optional RS-485 direction control (DE): 

import serial

# Open UART with RX=16, TX=17 at 115200 baud
u = serial(16, 17, 115200)

# Optional: configure RS-485 driver enable pin
u.config_tx_en(4)

# Write data
u.write("STATUS\r\n")

# Non-blocking read of staged bytes
if u.available() > 0
  var data = u.read()
  print("Received:", data)
end

u.close()

docs.title: Persistent Data Storage (import persist)
docs.text:
Stores dynamic script attributes safely in /_persist.json. Serialized data is bounded to 8192 bytes and 16 container levels, and saved atomically: 

import persist

persist.my_counter = persist.find("my_counter", 0) + 1
persist.device_label = "Living Room Sensor"

# In-place mutations to lists/maps require dirty() before save
persist.dirty()

# Saves dirty attributes immediately to LittleFS (also flushed before restart)
persist.save()

docs.title: Filesystem Navigation (import path)
docs.text:
Inspect and manage files on the LittleFS partition: 

import path

if path.exists("/display.ini")
  print("Display descriptor found")
end

# List direct children (bounded to 128 entries and 8192 bytes)
var files = path.listdir("/")
print("Files:", files)

path.remove("/temp.txt")
path.rename("/old.txt", "/new.txt")

docs.title: MQTT Scripting (import mqtt)
docs.text:
Publish messages and subscribe to topics with script callbacks across broker reconnects: 

import mqtt

if mqtt.connected()
  mqtt.publish("tele/mydevice/alert", "motion detected")
end

# Subscribe with callback handler
mqtt.subscribe("cmnd/mydevice/custom", def (topic, payload)
  print("Received MQTT command:", topic, payload)
end)

docs.title: Energy Meters (import energy)
docs.text:
With USE_BERRY_ENERGY_API (checked access to selected meter drivers) or USE_BERRY_ENERGY (a virtual meter fed by your script), import energy exposes the configured meter slots. Handles validate an identity generation on every access, so a removed or replaced instance needs a new handle:

import energy
var meter = energy.configure(1, 3)       # virtual meter in slot 1, 1–8 channels (durable)
meter.voltage = 230.0                    # volts
meter.current = 1.25                     # amps
meter.active_power = 287.5               # watts (negative = export)
meter.active_power_phases[1] = 120.0     # zero-based channel 2
print(meter.read())                      # copied map of all measurements

Hardware measurements are read-only; configure hardware meters with the normal energy commands. Scalars address channel 1, _2…_N suffixes or _phases views address the rest. Optional API flags add read-only Today/Yesterday projections and balanced sums.

docs.title: Dashboard Widgets (import widget)
docs.text:
With Berry and the web interface, import widget puts cards on the Home page.
