docs.title: Web Interface
docs.text: Your device hosts its own little website: open http://<device-ip>/ (the default on Compact and Standard profiles) or https://<device-ip>/ (the default on Large profiles) in a browser, sign in with the web password you set over serial (First Steps), and you get live status, lights and relays, sensor and energy readings, GPIO and timer editors, a file editor, and interactive consoles — no cloud, no app to install.

docs.title: A normal day in the browser
docs.text:
• Status at a glance: device identity, network address, memory, and filesystem usage refresh live (a small power snapshot every second, heavier details slower).
  • Switch things: relay cards flip your outputs, and each configured light gets its own card above them — same result as typing Power1 on or Dimmer 80 on the console. A relay that a light owns does not get a second switch.
  • Light cards: the controls follow the light's kind. A dimmer gets a brightness slider (plus a CT slider for tunable white); RGB lights get a colour wheel for hue and saturation, with a dimmer and a white or CT slider on RGBW and RGBCW lights. A mapped TuyaMCU mode also adds a white/colour button on RGBW and RGBCW lights. The wheel works from the keyboard (left/right change hue, up/down change saturation). As with Tasmota's Dimmer and Color, any nonzero brightness or a colour/CT change switches the light on, and brightness 0 switches it off while keeping the stored dimmer. Updates are sent at most every 150 ms per light, latest value wins, and are never retried.
  • Sensor and energy cards: when sensors are compiled, live temperature, humidity, pressure, and ambient light display with units and labels. Every BLE device gets its own card with RSSI, Battery, LastSeen and NMT in a footer; ages count up in the page. Each reading can show its last 24 hours as a small chart. With energy drivers, each meter instance gets its own card with a channel selector (meters are never added together).
  • Berry widgets: scripts using import widget add cards after the native ones. As in Tasmota, a script ships the card's HTML and JS; the page adds bindings, charts (lines, bars, gauges, QR codes), controls and styles, and shows the script's values only as text. At most 16 widgets, each with up to 4096 bytes of markup and 2816 bytes of data. The compact Beken page shows widgets too, with the dot-matrix and (with Matter) QR charts only. See Berry scripting.
  • Audio player: with USE_WEB_AUDIO and an I2S output in the template, Home shows the command session, source and playback state, with file or URL selection, pause, resume, stop and volume controls. Audio and codecs must be enabled in the build.
  • Matter card: with USE_MATTER, the Home page shows the Matter stack state. While a commissioning window is open it shows the fabric count, pairing code and a QR code; otherwise it offers Open commissioning window, and once a controller has joined, Remove all fabrics (with a second press to confirm). See Matter.
  • Configuration → Module and Template: edit GPIOs in Tasmota's two steps. Module picks a built-in module (or the user template, module 0) and assigns functions to the pins that template marks User. Template edits the user template itself (name, base, flag, one function per slot, User, or none), shows its JSON for copy and paste, and can activate it as Module 0. Pins that cannot support a function are not offered, reserved pins cannot be assigned, and duplicate functions block saving. Changes apply after a restart.
  • Configuration → Timer: lists all 16 Tasmota timers with the global Timers switch, and edits one timer at a time — active, mode (time of day, or sunrise/sunset with an offset up to 11:59), random window, weekdays, repeat, output, and action (off, on, toggle, Berry callback). A location card for Latitude, Longitude, and Sunrise appears when a timer uses sunrise or sunset. A warning shows while the device clock is not synchronized, because timers only fire with valid time. Unsaved edits are kept until you save or discard them.
  • Configuration → MQTT: broker settings, topics with live previews, retain options, and connection diagnostics, with explicit password keep/replace/clear. Saving a setting and the broker accepting the connection are reported separately. A Test runs a trial connection and restores the normal client afterwards.
  • Firmware Update: shows the running version and build. Update from URL saves OtaUrl and starts Upgrade 1; Upload firmware file restarts into the Safeboot recovery page (Restart 3) where the file is uploaded. See Install & Update.
  • Parallel Web & Berry Consoles: side-by-side consoles with separate input and output panes. The Web Console runs Newmota commands; the Berry Console runs Berry source in the persistent VM, up to 64 KiB. Inputs above the 2 KiB request-body size are sent in sequential chunks into a temporary heap buffer, released after compilation; source is never staged on flash. Each keeps the last 20 inputs (Up/Down); Berry preserves normal caret movement inside multiline source. Run with the button, Ctrl/Command+Enter, or Enter on a trailing blank line.
  • LittleFS File Browser and Editor: lists names, types, and sizes with per-file Edit and Delete (directories can be deleted when empty). Upload accepts several files, folder selection, and drag-and-drop; relative folder paths are kept, empty folders are not transferred. The editor handles UTF-8 text, new files, and Save As, normalizes line endings, and warns about unsaved changes. Transfers show progress and can be cancelled; an interrupted write keeps the existing file. Newmota's internal settings files are protected from browser reads and writes.
  • Onboarding Mode: when unconfigured or when the saved network fails, the device boots an open SoftAP named after its hostname, with the setup page at http://192.168.4.1 (https:// on HTTPS builds). You can scan networks and test credentials in the browser; they are committed only after association and DHCP succeed. There is no captive-portal redirect.
  • Panels that aren't ready are shown visibly disabled — the UI never shows fake values. (A Backup tab currently exists only as a mock-up.)

Each firmware embeds one language, chosen at build time from language/ through the environment's language field (English en_GB and German de_DE ship today); there is no runtime language switch. Command names, JSON keys, and MQTT topics stay in English. If a command's answer is too large for the small device buffers, the page tells you the command may have run rather than guessing — just check with Status.

HTTPS vs. HTTP profiles

  • Large profiles: serve HTTPS on port 443 by default, with Brotli-compressed assets and a per-device self-signed P-256 certificate generated on first start (kept at /.newmota/web-identity.bin, protected from browser access). Your browser will warn that no trusted CA issued it. A damaged identity is regenerated; if generation or TLS startup fails, the listener stays unavailable instead of falling back to HTTP.
  • Compact, Standard, and Safeboot profiles: serve HTTP on port 80 with Gzip-compressed assets.

Switch either default in a personal build with features: {USE_WEB_HTTPS: true} (or false). An HTTP build leaves out the TLS identity generator and server. crypto: none does not affect web TLS.

docs.title: Provisioning Access (WebPassword)
docs.text:
The listener starts after station networking is ready or the recovery SoftAP has a local address. A web password can be provisioned through the physical serial console:

WebPassword your-device-password
  • Use 8..64 bytes. The reply is always masked ({"WebPassword":"****"}).
  • Open the device address and sign in with that password.
  • WebPassword 0 clears the credential and leaves web access open without authentication, matching standard Tasmota behavior.
  • Password changes and settings resets invalidate all active sessions.
  • Initial provisioning and password replacement are serial-only — no shared factory password or unauthenticated remote password-change route exists.

docs.title: UI and API Architecture
docs.text:
The embedded responsive page is minified at build time — comments and layout whitespace are removed, and script and style bodies pass through rjsmin and rcssmin (they do not rename or rewrite code); pre and textarea content stays verbatim. It is then compressed (Brotli for HTTPS builds, Gzip for HTTP builds) and served verbatim; the device performs no runtime compression, so comments in index.html cost nothing on the device. The browser and the serial console share one command processor, and the page uses the same canonical STATE payload that feeds MQTT, so there is no second dashboard-only device model.

  • Fast snapshot: /api/state provides the small complete power snapshot; /api/light returns {"Lights":[…]} and accepts POST updates (endpoint plus any of power, bri, hue, sat, ct, rgb, channels).
  • Sensors: /api/sensors returns the canonical document; /api/sensors/readings returns typed values with labels and units. /api/sensors/updates returns only sensors with new data (plus more/reset/heap), and /api/sensors/updates/all marks everything first. /api/sensors/history/<series> returns one reading's last 24 hours as {"step":<seconds>,"values":[...]}. /api/energy and POST /api/energy/channel serve the meter cards.
  • Widgets: /api/widgets/updates/<since> answers what changed after a revision (every widget with its markup and data revisions, the changed data, the next revision and a per-boot generation), /api/widgets/markup/<id> returns a widget's markup, and POST /api/widgets/action takes id\nname\nvalue from a control and queues it for the script (503 when eight are waiting).
  • Bootstrap: /api/info provides authenticated read-only metadata for identity (the persisted DeviceName separate from the network hostname), network, memory, and LittleFS storage.
  • Hardware: /api/gpio/catalog and /api/gpio back the Module and Template editors; saves use the validated Module, GPIO, Template, and optional Restart 1 commands. /api/timers returns the timer switch, clock validity, location, and all 16 timers.
  • MQTT: GET/POST /api/mqtt, POST /api/mqtt/preview, GET /api/mqtt/status, and POST /api/mqtt/test.
  • Filesystem: POST /api/filesystem/list returns bounded directory pages; uploads, edits, and deletes use the transfer routes.
  • Consoles: POST /api/command submits a command; POST /api/console/command also returns the timestamped result to the sending page; POST /api/console/poll fetches bounded history; POST /api/berry/console (plus begin, chunk, run, abort for large sources) drives the Berry VM.
  • Bounds: two browser sessions; the listener's simultaneous connection count follows the platform adapter. Headers are limited to 2 KiB, command bodies to 512 bytes, and dynamic responses to 4 KiB. Berry input accepts up to 64 KiB of UTF-8 source, transferred in chunks; incomplete uploads expire after 30 seconds.
  • Session security: random session cookies, a separate CSRF token, Host/origin checks, and bounded connection counts. Commands are never retried automatically.

docs.title: Safeboot & Beken Recovery Web
docs.text:
Network-capable Safeboot images compile a dedicated recovery HTTP service:

  • Safeboot Recovery Page: Safeboot serves a compact, authenticated recovery page from /. Newmota application users enter it using Restart 3 (or the Firmware Update page) and reconnect after reboot.
  • Bounded Browser Upload: Firmware updates are uploaded in sequential binary chunks capped at 1 KiB, verified against checksum and layout constraints before activation.
  • Safety Checks: The recovery writer targets only the application slot (app0, OTA2, or equivalent) and never touches bootloader, partition metadata, or LittleFS. Safeboot requires a configured WebPassword and fails closed without it.
  • Beken Compact Root Page: Beken has no Safeboot, so its normal application embeds one smaller English-only page with the same sidebar, responsive panels, and four themes. Home shows light cards, one switch per relay that no light owns, and energy cards; Configuration has Wi-Fi, MQTT, Module, Template, and Timers tabs; Information and the file browser show LittleFS used, free, and total; and the native RBL updater requires acknowledging that LittleFS data may be lost. It follows the normal login policy, including open access when WebPassword is empty.

The web slice compiles on all five platform families. ESP32-S3, XH-CB3S/BK7238, BW16, and Pico 2 W have browser smoke evidence (which predates the current Beken page); BL602 has build and size evidence only, and end-to-end upload, reboot, and recovery behavior still need hardware testing.

docs.title: Web Flasher
docs.text:
The Web Flasher writes a Newmota factory package from the browser, without a build environment. Every build places the package next to its manifest, for example build/firmware/cb2s-2m/<version>/newmota-cb2s-2m-<version>-factory.zip. Load it below, connect the device and press Connect and write. It needs a desktop Chrome, Edge or other Chromium browser (Web Serial, and WebUSB for the Pico).

  • It writes the same regions as make flash-only PACKAGE=… and refuses the same cases: a flash smaller than the package, a chip other than the package's, Beken modules without RF calibration where the layout keeps it, and ESP chips with secure boot, flash encryption or secure download mode.
  • Back up the whole flash before writing is on by default. The backup downloads before anything is written; Back up only reads it without writing. Keep backups private: they can contain Wi-Fi credentials and device keys. AmebaD has no backup, as with make.
  • The baud rate defaults to the upload speed of make flash. After a successful write the serial monitor opens at the console speed; reset the board if it does not start by itself.
  • A Raspberry Pi Pico is written over USB in BOOTSEL mode: choose the board, and a board running Newmota switches to BOOTSEL by itself (then press the button again and choose the RP2 Boot device); otherwise hold BOOTSEL while plugging it in.

The flasher is not part of this build of the documentation. Build it with npm run build in flasher/.

The flasher is free software under the GNU GPL 3.0 or later. Its components and the loaders it sends to a chip, with their licenses, are listed in its THIRD_PARTY.md.

docs.title: AmebaD BW16 Devices
docs.text: Newmota on Realtek dual-core Wi-Fi + BLE microcontrollers (RTL8720D/DN, BW16 modules).

docs.title: Supported Microcontrollers
docs.text: • RTL8720DN / BW16 (Dual-core ARM Cortex-M0 + Cortex-M4 Wi-Fi/BLE module, 2 MiB Compact)

docs.title: Dual-Core Build Lifecycle
docs.text:
The AmebaD platform adapter (tools/newmota/platforms/amebad/build.py) orchestrates vendor Makefile compilation for both onboard CPU cores:

  1. KM0 Core (Cortex-M0): Low-power engine and boot controller.
  2. KM4 Core (Cortex-M4): High-performance application core running Newmota's C++ core (src/app/core/) and RTOS services.
# Build the baseline BW16 2 MiB environment (plus its safeboot companion)
make bw16-2m

The bw16-2m application environment declares safeboot: bw16-2m-safeboot; the pipeline builds the safeboot image first, then the application.

docs.title: Serial Makefile Execution
docs.text: Because AmebaD SDK Makefiles share clean and build targets that race under parallel make, the platform adapter executes native AmebaD builds serially while retaining parallel job execution for single-core targets.

docs.title: Output Artifacts
docs.text: A successful build generates the vendor KM0, KM4, combined image, AXF, and map under build/work/bw16-2m/. The packager (tools/newmota/platforms/amebad/images.py, device driver device.py, host uploader uploader.py) writes a paired factory package under build/firmware/bw16-2m/<version>/ containing the Safeboot and application image2 outputs, both boot images, an empty 64 KiB LittleFS image, the pinned flashloader, and the community Python write/verify uploader plan with manifest + SHA-256 hashes.

docs.title: 2 MiB Factory Layout
docs.text:
The factory layout follows the ESP 2 MiB split, with boot images retained at 0x0000 and 0x4000:

Region Offset Size Content Boot images 0x0000, 0x4000 — Vendor boot images (retained) Safeboot / OTA1 0x010000 0x0C8000 Safeboot image2 Application / OTA2 0x0D8000 0x118000 Application image2 LittleFS 0x1F0000 0x10000 (64 KiB) Filesystem (native adapter)

The factory path verifies the flashloader's word-sum checksums. The package manifest records hashes before any device is opened.

docs.title: Wired Operations
docs.text:
# Factory flash. Enter UART download mode when prompted,
# then reset the board manually after verification.
# Use an explicit port while this path is experimental.
make flash ENV=bw16-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

# Update: writes only the coupled KM0/KM4 application image into OTA2.
# Enter UART download mode when prompted, then reset manually.
# A device currently in Safeboot remains there (boot selection is preserved).
make update ENV=bw16-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

Upload runs at 230400 baud and the console at 115200 (override with BAUD/MONITOR_BAUD). probe and backup are not available.

make update runs the SDK's coupled KM0/KM4 build and writes only the combined application image to OTA2. It does not build Safeboot or a filesystem package and is not the signed remote OTA implementation.

docs.title: Web & Network Services
docs.text:
AmebaD is the second native web port after ESP32-C2: Wi-Fi application builds serve the shared HTTP+Gzip UI through Realtek's native HTTPD library (src/platform/amebad/web.cpp) behind the same bounded web.h application interface. The 2 MiB Compact image serves HTTP; HTTPS is an opt-in build feature (USE_WEB_HTTPS), and browser-behavior hardware testing remains pending. See Web Interface.

SoftAP onboarding (192.168.4.1): the latest BW16 log confirms station and AP operation, the 192.168.4.1 address, DHCP, and scan results. Browser onboarding routes and AP restart mode need a hardware retest, and scan warnings during multi-channel concurrency and client stability remain open. MQTT operates over the shared TCP transport layer (src/platform/lwip/tcp_stream.cpp), the same as on ESP32. See MQTT & Telemetry for configuration.

docs.title: Hardware testing
docs.text:
Seen on BW16 hardware: factory write/verify, manual reset, clean LittleFS 2.0 initialization, settings persistence, Wi-Fi/NTP startup, setup AP with DHCP and scanning, serial monitoring, and Restart 3 image switching. The OTA1/OTA2 layout above is newer than the earlier trials, so browser onboarding and the current update layout still need testing.

Still open: make probe and make backup (unavailable), OTA2-only update testing, recovery, automated reset, and broader testing. See Build System Internals and Console & Commands (Restart 3) for what each operation writes.

docs.title: Beken Devices
docs.text: Newmota on Beken ARM Wi-Fi microcontrollers — the chips inside countless Tuya modules (CB2S, CB3S, CBU, WB2S, XH-CB3S). One warning up front: on Beken an update can erase your stored files, keeping only Wi-Fi credentials — see Files & Settings.

docs.title: Supported Microcontrollers
docs.text:
• BK7231N (Primary non-ESP Compact target; QFN32 2 MiB/4 MiB) — environments cb2s-2m, cb3s
  • BK7238 (distinct SoC profile) — environment xh-cb3s (do not use cb3s for XH-CB3S hardware)
  • BK7231T — environment wb2s; generic Tuya QFN32 board recipe also available.
  • BK7252 / BK7252N — generic-bk7252-2m, generic-bk7252-4m, generic-bk7252n-2m, and generic-bk7252n-4m, for the Beken SDK bootloader.
  • BK7231Q / BK7251 — board recipes are present; use a matching target profile.

docs.title: Native Build & Toolchain
docs.text:
The platform adapter (tools/newmota/platforms/beken/build.py, with specialist helpers bdk.py, codec.py, profile.py) drives the BDK Make-based pipeline over the pinned framework-beken-bdk v3.0.78 (the Newmota/framework-beken-bdk fork; Newmota's own sources build with -Wall):

  • Integrates native chip defaults (config/build/beken/<target>/defconfig) with the resolved SoC profile.
  • Compiles C++ code (src/app/core/) alongside Beken platform bindings (src/platform/beken/), including the native LittleFS adapter (filesystem.cpp), flash access layer (flash_access.cpp), OTA-critical settings bridge (critical_settings.cpp, net_param_tlv.cpp), and BDK compatibility shims (native/bdk_compat.c, native/libc_heap.c, native/libc_syscalls.c). Standard output and error go to the log UART.
  • Produces a native AXF/raw diagnostic image, a CRC-wrapped application RBL for wired flashing, and an OpenBeken-style compressed/encrypted RBL for single-image OTA staging.
# Build the baseline BK7231N CB2S environment
make cb2s-2m

# Build the BK7238 XH-CB3S environment
make xh-cb3s

The Beken and AmebaD Make-based builds record their real cross-compiler invocations for clangd and may compile/relink the staged native project to obtain them. No platform substitutes a host compiler.

docs.title: Storage Model
docs.text:
Beken uses a bounded OpenBeken-style LittleFS tail overlay inside the native OTA staging envelope (config/partitions/beken/2m.toml, 2m-bk7238.toml, 4m.toml). OTA may erase that filesystem — this overlap is deliberate.

The portable OTA-critical record keeps both Wi-Fi slots outside that overlay through an opaque Beken NET-parameter adapter (net_param_tlv.cpp), which preserves co-resident native records. Retention across OTA remains untested. Settings otherwise live in the LittleFS overlay; there is no Newmota Safeboot or alternate-image package on Beken — Safeboot support is intentionally deferred, and recovery scope is stock OTA plus physical/ROM recovery.

docs.title: Runtime Console
docs.text:
Beken uses the SDK's selected log UART for both logs and commands: UART1 on the current BK7231N and BK7238 BDK profiles. Newmota polls the SDK's interrupt-fed software receive FIFO; command parsing and execution stay in the common serial transport. When TuyaMCU uses UART1, the serial console is unavailable. Typed characters are not echoed — enter a command such as Status followed by Enter.

The BK7238/XH-CB3S path has passed initial command-input hardware smoke testing; other exact-board combinations and other consoles have not yet been tested.

docs.title: Wired Operations
docs.text:
The pinned bk7231tools writer (v2.1.2, device support) handles chip/flash probing, complete backup, aligned write/verify, and chip reboot. Upload runs at 1500000 baud and the console at 115200 (override with BAUD/MONITOR_BAUD).

flash, flash-monitor, and both flash-only forms install fresh Newmota configuration: they initialize LittleFS and remove Newmota's Wi-Fi credentials from the NET records. Native NET vendor records are retained, and foreign non-TLV configuration is replaced with an empty native table. A damaged native table or too little credential space stops the operation before any write. The bootloader, RF calibration, device identity, and BLE bonding are preserved. A package built before this policy existed must be rebuilt.

# Beken: use the module's UART1/download pins for the programmer.
# The first operation must be a complete backup; this preserves the stock
# bootloader and metadata.
make probe ENV=cb2s-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001
make backup ENV=cb2s-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001 OUTPUT=cb2s-stock.bin
make flash ENV=cb2s-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

# XH-CB3S/BK7238 uses its own exact environment; do not use `cb3s` for it.
make probe ENV=xh-cb3s PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001
make backup ENV=xh-cb3s PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001 OUTPUT=xh-cb3s-stock.bin
make flash ENV=xh-cb3s PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

# Beken development update: writes only stock OTA staging and may erase the LittleFS tail.
make update ENV=cb2s-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001
make update ENV=xh-cb3s PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

docs.title: Web & Network Services
docs.text:
BK7231N and BK7238 environments compile the device-hosted HTTP web service and bounded plain MQTT client:

  • Compact Beken Web Page: Beken embeds one smaller, English-only root page rather than the full generic UI. It has the same sidebar, responsive panels, and four themes, with Home (light cards with colour wheel, dimmer and white/CT slider, one switch per relay no light owns, and energy cards), Configuration tabs (Wi-Fi, MQTT, Module, Template, Timers), Information and a filesystem browser with LittleFS used/free/total, a console, and the native RBL updater. Firmware update requests are sent in 1 KiB chunks and verified before activation. Updating requires acknowledging that LittleFS data may be lost.
  • Onboarding AP: Boots an open newmota-XXXXXX SoftAP (192.168.4.1) when unconfigured, allowing network setup and credential testing from any browser.
  • No BLE Adapter: Newmota does not drive the Beken Bluetooth LE radio. USE_BLE and USE_BLE_SENSORS are unavailable on BK7231 targets, so no BLE sensors are decoded here.
  • MQTT & Telemetry: Full Tasmota-compatible MQTT client and periodic telemetry reports over plain IPv4 TCP.
  • Feature limits: Beken does not compile WS2812 (its pinned DMA waveform path could violate the WS2812B LOW limit), I2S audio, or QSPI displays, and its native SPI display selectors are rejected; software SPI, I2C, EPD, and GPIO I80 displays work where the module exposes enough pads.

docs.title: Hardware testing
docs.text:
The XH-CB3S/BK7238 path has passed hardware testing for its core stack: stable boot/restart, UART1 commands, LittleFS mount/read, Wi-Fi station association, DHCP, NTP synchronization, full HTTP web UI, web console, and Wi-Fi onboarding handoff.

Still open: update retention, complete backup/recovery, filesystem survival across OTA, GPIO topology, and repeated power-loss behavior — plus equivalent testing on the other Beken boards. What each wired operation writes is described in Build System Internals.

docs.title: Bouffalo Devices
docs.text: Newmota targets Bouffalo Lab RISC-V microcontrollers with the pinned BouffaloSDK v2.3.34 (the Newmota/bouffalo_sdk fork, which carries the Wi-Fi 6 and warning fixes Newmota needs).

docs.title: Supported Microcontrollers
docs.text:
Environment Chip Flash Profile bl602-2m BL602 (RISC-V Wi-Fi 4 + BLE) 2 MiB Compact bl602-4m BL602 4 MiB Standard bl616dk BL616 (Wi-Fi 6) 4 MiB Standard bl618dgdk BL618DG (Wi-Fi 6, single-core) 4 MiB Standard

Each application environment is paired with its own Safeboot image. BL702 is cataloged as planned and has no Newmota native build adapter.

BL618DG is low priority. It builds and is packaged with the code it shares with BL616, but is not tested on hardware and gets no BL618DG-specific features.

Note

BL618 modules. bl618dgdk targets the BL618DG chip only. Modules such as the Ai-M61-32S are BL616-family silicon: use bl616dk and a GPIO template. The earlier bl618dk environment was renamed bl618dgdk.

docs.title: Native Build Lifecycle
docs.text:
The Bouffalo platform adapter (tools/newmota/platforms/bouffalo/build.py) invokes BouffaloSDK's CMake build system and linker scripts. Partition maps are selected by SDK target: 2m.toml for the BL602 Compact layout, and 4m-bl602.toml, 4m-bl616.toml, or 4m-bl618dg.toml for the 4 MiB targets. Each application build also builds its paired Safeboot image and packages the layout.

make bl602-2m
make bl602-4m
make bl616dk
make bl618dgdk

BL616 and BL618DG use the SDK's FHOST Wi-Fi 6 manager with FreeRTOS and lwIP. Both are Standard applications with the paired Safeboot, and their setup AP is served from 192.168.4.1 with DHCP, like every other family. SDK logging is forced to none in the BL602, BL616, and BL618DG Safeboot images so they fit their recovery partitions.

docs.title: Apple Silicon toolchain note
docs.text: Bouffalo setup downloads the pinned native Xuantie GCC 14 release from Newmota/bouffalo-toolchain-macos-arm64. Its macOS binaries include their host dependencies; a separate Homebrew runtime-library install is not required. Device operations use the pinned blflashcommand Python package (installed by make uv-setup), so Apple Silicon needs no Rosetta.

docs.title: BL602 2 MiB Layout
docs.text:
Region Offset Size Content Boot2 0x000000 0x00E000 Bootloader Partition tables 0x00E000 / 0x00F000 — Redundant CRC-protected copies Application (FW slot 0) 0x010000 0x14C000 Normal firmware Safeboot (FW slot 1) 0x15C000 0x094000 Recovery image LittleFS (lfs) 0x1F0000 0x010000 (64 KiB) Persistent filesystem region

The Compact layout contains only the regions Newmota owns: it omits the SDK's unused manufacturing, media, PSM, key, and factory regions so the application gets the contiguous space in front of Safeboot. Restart 3 flips the active slot through a CRC-protected partition-table update, which is safe across interruption.

docs.title: Four MiB Layouts
docs.text:
BL602, BL616, and BL618DG each have a target-specific map. All reserve the final 320 KiB for LittleFS:

Region BL602 4 MiB BL616 / BL618DG 4 MiB Content Boot2 0x000000 – 0x00E000 0x000000 – 0x00E000 Bootloader Partition tables 0x00E000 / 0x00F000 0x00E000 / 0x00F000 Redundant CRC-protected copies Application (FW slot 0) 0x010000, size 0x2A0000 0x010000, size 0x260000 Standard firmware Safeboot (FW slot 1) 0x2B0000, size 0x100000 0x270000, size 0x140000 Recovery image LittleFS (lfs) 0x3B0000, size 0x050000 0x3B0000, size 0x050000 Persistent filesystem (320 KiB)

The BL602 hardware trial did not make LittleFS or settings available, so these regions are layout budgets, not hardware-tested storage capacity. A device carrying an older layout needs a complete factory package before application-only updates are accepted.

docs.title: Wired Operations
docs.text:
make probe ENV=bl602-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001
make backup ENV=bl602-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001 OUTPUT=bl602-stock.bin
make flash ENV=bl602-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001
make update ENV=bl602-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001
  • Upload runs at 500000 baud by default; the console runs at 2000000 baud on UART0 (override with BAUD and MONITOR_BAUD).
  • Writes are verified by the loader's SHA-256 check. probe validates both partition-table copies (one valid copy is accepted) and cannot tell a BL616 from a BL618: the environment selects the chip profile.
  • backup reads the declared flash size.
  • update writes only the application slot; boot2, both partition-table copies, Safeboot, vendor regions, and LittleFS are untouched, and the FW active index is preserved, so a device in Safeboot stays there.

docs.title: Wi-Fi Supplicant on BearSSL
docs.text:
USE_WIFI_WPA3_BEARSSL is on by default in every Bouffalo Wi-Fi build (BL602, BL616, BL618DG), together with USE_CRYPTO_HW_SHA1. To go back to the SDK's mbedTLS supplicant, turn it off in a personal build:

name: bl616dk-mbedtls
inherit: bl616dk
features:
  USE_WIFI_WPA3_BEARSSL: false
  • BL616 and BL618DG: the Wi-Fi 6 supplicant runs on BearSSL instead of mbedTLS, WPA3-SAE included. SAE offers group 19 (P-256) only; an access point that allows only groups 20 or 21 cannot be joined.
  • BL602: only the supplicant's MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 move to BearSSL; SAE stays on the SDK's own crypto.
  • The Wi-Fi key (PSK) is derived on the chip's SHA-1 engine: 4096 PBKDF2 iterations take 48.5 ms on BL616 and 63.5 ms on BL602.
  • Without HTTPS the image links no mbedTLS. Application images are 16,400 B smaller on BL602 (bl602-2m) and 20,800 B on BL616 (bl616dk); Safeboot images are 11,376 B smaller on BL602, 13,424 B on BL616 and 14,928 B on BL618DG.
  • BL602 and BL616 joined a network with it; BL618DG is untested on hardware.
  • Please report: after joining a WPA3 network with a BL616 build that has this option, the console shows a line like WIF: supplicant stack free 6144 of 12288 B (the first number varies). Please send that line, with the access point's WPA3 mode (WPA3-only or WPA2/WPA3 transition), once the Newmota issue tracker opens in the alpha stage. It tells us whether the supplicant's 12 KiB stack is large enough; the line will be removed once there is a report.

docs.title: Peripheral Limits
docs.text:
Feature BL602 BL616 BL618DG PWM Yes (GPIO n → channel n % 5) Yes, PWM-v2 (GPIO n → channel n % 4, one shared carrier) Unavailable WS2812 strip Yes Unavailable Unavailable I2S audio No peripheral Unavailable Unavailable ADC, auxiliary UART, native display SPI Native display SPI0 available Unavailable Unavailable Display (USE_DISPLAY_QSPI) Rejected Yes Yes (signal order provisional)

Two PWM pins that map to the same channel cannot run together, because the channels share one divider and period. General GPIO display transports stay available on every Bouffalo chip.

docs.title: Ready-Made Templates
docs.text: Templates for the Ai-Thinker Ai-M61-32S-Kit, Ai-M62-12F-Kit, and Ai-WB2-12F-Kit (RGB indicator on PWM pins, driven as a dimmable RGB light) are in the firmware repository's TEMPLATE.md. Test one with Color FF0000 or Dimmer 20.

docs.title: Hardware testing
docs.text: The attached BL602 board passed a factory write with device read-back and booted to its setup AP and HTTP listener; the boot console still reported WEB: HTTPS identity or server start failed on the BL602 4 MiB adapter. Probe/backup testing, LittleFS/settings, browser UI, Safeboot recovery, and application-only updates remain open. BL602 and BL616 joined a network with the standard build, which has the BearSSL supplicant; BL618DG has compile/package evidence only.

docs.title: Build Your Firmware
docs.text:
Newmota has no ready-made downloads yet, so the first step is to build an image for your device on your own computer. You don't need to edit code for this: make config lets you pick your chip and features from a menu, checks that the combination works, and then builds it.

Wi-Fi, MQTT, GPIO templates and other device settings are not part of the image. You set them later on the device, through the web interface or console commands, as in Tasmota. New terms such as environment or profile are explained in the Glossary.

Coming from Tasmota?

Tasmota offers ready-made binaries for most devices and tailored builds through user_config_override.h. In Newmota, the interactive make config takes the place of both: choose a starting environment, switch features on or off, and build.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A macOS or Linux computer.
  • Python 3.10 or newer, git and make.
  • uv, the Python package manager (installation guide).

Get the source and set up the project's Python environment:

git clone https://github.com/Newmota/Newmota.git
cd Newmota
make uv-setup

You don't need to install any compilers or vendor SDKs yourself. The first build for a platform downloads and installs its toolchain and SDK, which takes a while. Later builds reuse them.

docs.title: Find your environment
docs.text:
An environment is a checked-in build target: chip, flash size, profile and the board's layout. Supported Devices and the platform guides name the environment for each board. To see the full list:

make list

To use an environment exactly as it is, you can skip make config and build it straight away, for example make esp32c3-4m.

docs.title: Configure with make config
docs.text:
make config                    # choose everything from the menu
make config ENV=esp32c3-4m     # start from this environment

The configurator runs in the terminal and has four tabs:

Tab What you do there Target Choose the platform family, then the chip and the environment to start from. Set the profile, the language and the name of your build. Features Switch optional features on or off, such as sensors, displays, BLE or Matter. / filters the list. Summary Preview the file that will be written. Help Keys and markers.

Each feature shows why it is on or off:

Marker Meaning [*] You selected it. [=] The base environment already has it. [+] A feature you selected needs it, so it is on as well. [ ] Off. [-] Not available on this target; the detail line says why.

Selecting a feature brings in its dependencies, and features that your chip, flash size or board cannot support are blocked. Problems therefore show up while you choose, not halfway through a long build.

Press w to write the configuration, or b to write it and build it right away. q quits and asks first if you have unsaved changes.

Your build is saved as user_config/<name>.yaml, a short file that git ignores:

# User build configuration written by `make config`.
# Build it with: make build ENV=my-c3
name: my-c3
inherit: esp32c3-4m
features:
  USE_BME280: true
# Selected automatically through dependencies: USE_I2C

To change it later, run make config ENV=my-c3. Settings the menu doesn't offer, such as built-in Berry drivers or files for the factory filesystem, can be added to the file by hand and are kept when you reopen it. See Personal Build Configurations.

docs.title: Without the menu
docs.text:
The same steps work from a script or another tool:

# Show every feature and its state for an environment
uv run python tools/menuconfig.py --env esp32c3-4m --list-features

# Write user_config/my-c3.yaml with a BME280 sensor
uv run python tools/menuconfig.py --env esp32c3-4m --enable USE_BME280 --name my-c3 --write

# Build it
uv run python tools/menuconfig.py --env my-c3 --build

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
make my-c3

make build ENV=my-c3 does the same. Checked-in environments build the same way, for example make esp32c3-4m.

The finished package lands in build/firmware/<environment>/<version>/. It contains the manifest that make flash uses and the newmota-<environment>-<version>-factory.zip that you can load into the Web Flasher.

docs.text:

  • Web Flasher: write the factory package from the browser.
  • First Steps: connect the device to Wi-Fi.
  • Build From Source: toolchains, test matrices and build variables, for contributors.

docs.title: ESP32 Devices
docs.text: Newmota on Espressif ESP32 chips (ESP32, C2/C3/C5/C6/C61, S2/S3/S31, P4/P4X, H2) using upstream ESP-IDF v5.5 or v6.1. This is the leading platform: if a feature exists anywhere, it exists here first. All ESP32 builds carry the device-hosted web interface, LittleFS file browser, Berry console, MQTT, and Safeboot recovery.

docs.title: Supported Microcontrollers
docs.text:
• ESP32 (Classic dual-core Wi-Fi + BLE)
  • ESP32-C2 (Ultra-low-cost RISC-V 2 MiB Wi-Fi + BLE)
  • ESP32-C3 (Mainstream RISC-V 4 MiB Wi-Fi + BLE)
  • ESP32-C5 / ESP32-C6 / ESP32-C61 (Dual-band 2.4/5GHz Wi-Fi 6 + Thread/Zigbee/BLE)
  • ESP32-S2 / ESP32-S3 / ESP32-S31 (High-performance Xtensa LX7 with USB-OTG / CDC & OPI/QSPI PSRAM; S31 defaults to IDF 6.1 and is an SDK preview whose bootloader accepts images with an invalid SHA-256 hash: bring-up only)
  • ESP32-P4 / ESP32-P4X (High-performance RISC-V application SoC; P4X is revision 3.x silicon, maps to SDK target esp32p4, and defaults to IDF 6.1)
  • ESP32-H2 (IEEE 802.15.4 + BLE 5 leaf node)

docs.title: Build & Flashing Pipeline
docs.text: ESP-IDF targets use idf.py and CMake directly through Newmota's Python platform adapter (tools/newmota/platforms/esp/build.py).

docs.title: Native Packaging & Safeboot Pairing
docs.text:
A successful ESP-IDF build writes an immutable development factory package under build/firmware/<environment>/<version>/:

build/firmware/esp32c2-2m/<version>/
├── manifest.json       # Immutable package manifest with SHA-256 checksums
├── bootloader.bin      # ESP-IDF compiled bootloader
├── partition-table.bin # Compiled partition table
├── factory.bin         # Combined factory flash image
└── filesystem.bin      # Pre-generated LittleFS partition image

Environments declare explicit roles (application vs safeboot under config/env/esp-idf/<role>/). When building an application with a declared safeboot dependency (e.g. esp32s3-qio-qspi referencing esp32s3-qio-qspi-safeboot), the build pipeline automatically compiles and verifies the safeboot image before producing the final application package.

At runtime, Newmota supports Tasmota-compatible partition switching via the Restart 3 command. When triggered on an ESP-IDF target with a single-OTA Tasmota partition table, it updates the otadata boot sector to toggle between app0 and safeboot without manual reflashing.

docs.title: Dynamic Partition Auto-Scaling
docs.text:
When flashing an ESP32 target with make flash ENV=<env>, Newmota probes the physical flash chip size via esptool. If the physical chip capacity exceeds the package layout (for example, a 4 MiB device running a 2 MiB package), Newmota automatically regenerates a temporary partition table:

  1. Keeps fixed bootloader, app, and system offsets unchanged.
  2. Expands only the trailing LittleFS filesystem partition to utilize remaining physical space.
  3. Writes the resized partition table and extended filesystem image safely.

A device smaller than the package is rejected. Probe data and the exact write plan are kept under build/work/<environment>/flash/<size>/. Flash-only setup installs ESP-IDF's pinned Python programming and monitoring environment without a compiler.

docs.title: Serial Console & USB Hardware Workflow
docs.text: ESP-IDF builds use a single application console for both system logs and interactive commands (src/platform/esp-idf/console.cpp).

docs.title: Dynamic USB vs. UART0 Console Detection
docs.text:
For boards configured with on-chip USB (usb-cdc or usb-serial-jtag, such as ESP32-S3):

  • During boot, Newmota actively monitors the USB hardware Start-of-Frame (SOF) counter for up to 250 ms.
  • If an active USB host connection is detected, the firmware activates the USB console.
  • If no host activity occurs within 250 ms, it cleanly falls back to UART0 for the lifetime of the boot session.
  • A board recipe with console: uart0 skips the USB probe entirely.

docs.title: Control-Line-Safe USB Monitor
docs.text:
Standard ESP-IDF monitor toggles DTR and RTS lines upon opening serial ports. On the ESP32-S3's built-in USB Serial/JTAG port (303a:1001), this assertion sequence forces the chip back into the ROM bootloader instead of attaching to the running application.

Newmota implements a custom control-line-safe launcher (tools/newmota/platforms/esp/usb_monitor.py):

  • No DTR/RTS Assertion: Attaches to the serial stream without modifying flow control lines.
  • Watchdog Reset: Flashing operations on USB Serial/JTAG finish with an explicit esptool watchdog_reset, cleanly booting the newly written SPI application before the monitor attaches.
  • USB Re-enumeration: The -monitor targets wait for the USB device to re-enumerate post-flash before attaching.
  • External UART adapters continue using standard hardware reset behavior.

The built-in USB Serial/JTAG controller (303a:1001) is not the same as native USB-OTG CDC (303a:0009). The S3 recipes follow Tasmota and use USB Serial/JTAG; their ser variants use UART0. USB-OTG CDC is not a generic S3 default, because with the internal PHY it needs the USB_PHY_SEL eFuse or hardware with a separately wired external PHY. MONITOR_PORT and MONITOR_BAUD also apply after re-enumeration.

docs.title: Web & Telemetry Services
docs.text: Normal Wi-Fi ESP-IDF application builds include the device-hosted web service (UI, LittleFS file browser, and dual Web/Berry consoles) via the native ESP-IDF HTTP/HTTPS server, as well as bounded plain MQTT client and telemetry services. Every ESP-IDF application has an exact-board Safeboot environment, including the 2 MiB ESP32-C2 target (esp32c2-2m + esp32c2-2m-safeboot).

docs.title: Capacity & Feature Allocation
docs.text:
• 2 MiB Targets (e.g. esp32c2-2m): Both application and Safeboot fit their partition budgets; served via HTTP+Gzip on port 80; WPA3-SAE is omitted to conserve flash.
  • 4 MiB+ Targets (e.g. esp32c3-4m, esp32s3-qio-opi): Served via HTTP+Gzip on port 80 (Standard profile); Large profiles (ESP32-P4, ESP32-S31, esp32s3-qio-opi-8m-8m) default to HTTPS on port 443 with Brotli-compressed assets and a self-signed certificate. Either default can be flipped with USE_WEB_HTTPS. Both retain full WPA3-SAE, BearSSL crypto module, and large LittleFS filesystems.
  • WPA3 on BearSSL: On both ESP-IDF tracks, chips with their own Wi-Fi radio run the Wi-Fi supplicant on BearSSL with their SHA-1, SHA-256 and P-256 hardware instead of the SDK's mbedTLS (USE_WIFI_WPA3_BEARSSL, on by default in application and Safeboot). Images without HTTPS then link no mbedTLS and are smaller (esp32c3: 1,137,792 B instead of 1,214,208 B). On ESP32-S31 (6.1 track) the Safeboot image shrinks from 958,304 B to 837,296 B. It needs the Newmota ESP-IDF fork, which the build checks out for both tracks. ESP32-P4 and ESP32-P4X reach Wi-Fi through ESP-Hosted, where the companion chip runs the supplicant, so they keep their previous setup, as does ESP32-H2. Set USE_WIFI_WPA3_BEARSSL: false in a personal build for the mbedTLS supplicant.
  • Dual ESP-IDF Tracks: Targets default to the pinned ESP-IDF 5.5 track. Environments or personal configs can select the 6.1 track via idf_version: "6.1" (default on ESP32-S31).
  • Matter & BLE: Both are implemented but no checked-in profile selects them. USE_MATTER needs at least 4 MiB flash and hardware entropy and runs only on ESP-IDF here; USE_MATTER_BLE additionally selects USE_BLE. Add them in a personal build, then enable Matter with SetOption151 1 and restart. See Matter and Bluetooth & BLE Sensors.
  • Settings Migration: The Tasmota 15.5.0.2 settings importer supports all eight ESP targets (ESP32, S2, S3, C2, C3, C5, C6, and P4), copying preserved Wi-Fi slots, preferred slot, and compatible web passwords on first boot.

docs.title: First Steps With Your Device
docs.text: From a freshly flashed device to a working smart-home gadget in about fifteen minutes. You need a USB/serial cable and a terminal program (or the make monitor command from the install guide).

docs.title: 1. Talk to it over serial
docs.text:
Connect the cable and open the console:

make monitor ENV=<your-env> PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

Type Status and press Enter. You should get a JSON answer. Two device quirks to know:

  • Commands are case-insensitive (status, STATUS, Status all work).
  • On Beken modules (CB2S/CB3S…) typed characters are not echoed — type blind and press Enter.

docs.title: 2. Connect it to your Wi-Fi
docs.text: You have two easy ways to get your device onto your home Wi-Fi:

docs.title: Option A: Onboarding SoftAP (No Cable Needed)
docs.text: When the device starts without configured credentials, it automatically spins up an open Wi-Fi network named newmota-XXXXXX (derived from its MAC address): 1. Connect to newmota-XXXXXX on your phone or laptop. 2. Open http://192.168.4.1/ in your browser (https://192.168.4.1/ on builds with HTTPS, where you must accept the self-signed certificate warning). There is no captive portal, so type the address yourself. 3. Scan for networks, enter your passphrase, test the connection, and apply.

docs.title: Option B: Over the Serial Cable
docs.text:
Give it your network directly from the terminal (slot 1 is primary, slot 2 is fallback):

SSId1 MyHomeNetwork
Password1 my-secret-password

Check that it joined:

Status 5
{"StatusNET":{"Hostname":"newmota-A1B2","IPAddress":"192.168.1.50",...}}

Note the IPAddress — that's where your device lives on your local network.

docs.title: 3. Set the web password (serial only)
docs.text:
To protect your device, WebPassword can only be set over the physical cable — never over the network:

WebPassword choose-something-long
{"WebPassword":"****"}

(The reply is always masked. WebPassword 0 leaves web access open without authentication.)

docs.title: 4. Open it in your browser
docs.text: Go to http://<device-ip>/ (https:// on Large profiles or builds with USE_WEB_HTTPS) and sign in with your web password. You'll see live device status, relay switches, and a console where you can type the same commands as over serial. Full tour: Web Interface.

docs.title: 5. Tell it what hardware it is
docs.text:
A generic firmware doesn't know whether pin 4 drives a relay or a button. Pick the closest ready-made definition, or describe your device:

Modules
Module 3

No match? Paste a Tasmota-style template or adjust single pins — the whole workflow is in Setting Up Your Device Hardware.

docs.title: 6. Switch something and make it stick
docs.text:
Power1 on
PowerOnState 3

PowerOnState 3 restores the last relay state after a power cut — the setting most people want. Timers (PulseTime), blink, and mutual-exclusion (Interlock) are in Relays, Buttons & LEDs.

docs.title: 7. Save a copy of your setup
docs.text:
• Copy your Template JSON somewhere safe — it's your whole hardware description in one line.
  • Keep the full-flash backup file you took during installation — it's your way back to stock.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Daily command reference: Console & Commands
  • What's on the filesystem and what survives updates: Files & Settings
  • Coming from Tasmota? Read Coming from Tasmota before assuming anything.

docs.title: Switching From Tasmota
docs.text:
This page moves an ESP32 device that runs Tasmota to Newmota. If your device runs something else, or you want a clean start, flash it over a cable as described in Install & Update Firmware and set it up with First Steps.

Tasmota is a mature, widely used firmware, and Newmota is a young pre-alpha project that follows its commands and templates. Keep that in mind before you replace a working Tasmota device: choose one you can open and reflash over a cable if something goes wrong.

Not tested end to end yet

The update from Tasmota and the import of its settings are built into every supported Newmota ESP image, but a full trial on a device is still open. Expect rough edges and keep a cable at hand.

docs.title: Two ways to switch
docs.text:
Over the air, from Tasmota's web page Over a cable Chips ESP32, S2, S3, C2, C3, C5, C6, P4 Every supported chip Wi-Fi and web password Taken over from Tasmota Set again Tasmota's filesystem Kept Replaced Tasmota's Safeboot Stays installed Replaced by Newmota's Safeboot Newmota's own update path (Upgrade 1) Not available until a factory flash Available

Either way, templates, GPIO assignments, MQTT and all other settings are not taken over. Write them down first, as described in the next section.

docs.title: 1. Note what you want to keep
docs.text:
On the Tasmota console, run these and copy the answers to a text file:

Command What it shows Template The device template: the pin layout of your plug, switch or bulb Module Whether the template is active (0 means the template is used) MqttHost, MqttPort, MqttUser, Topic The MQTT connection. The password is not shown; have it at hand DeviceName The name your smart home shows Timezone The time zone

Newmota understands the same commands, the same template JSON and the same GPIO function numbers, so you can paste the answers back later. The Coming from Tasmota page lists where Newmota differs.

docs.title: 2. Build the Newmota image
docs.text:
Build an environment with the same chip and flash size as the device, as described in Build Your Firmware. Tasmota's Status 2 shows the chip and Status 4 the flash size.

The image for the over-the-air path is in the build's ota/ folder:

build/firmware/<environment>/<version>/ota/newmota-<environment>-<version>-ota.bin

docs.title: 3a. Switch over the air
docs.text:
1. Open the Tasmota web page and go to Firmware Upgrade.
  2. Under Use file upload, choose the -ota.bin file from step 2 and press Start upgrade. For a large file Tasmota shows Switching to safeboot partition and continues in its Safeboot; if the Safeboot page asks for the file again, choose the same file.
  3. The device restarts into Newmota. On the first start with default settings, Newmota reads the Wi-Fi networks, the preferred network and the web password from Tasmota's settings and joins your Wi-Fi.
  4. Find the device on your network as before and open it in the browser.

What Newmota imports:

  • Both Wi-Fi networks (SSId1/Password1, SSId2/Password2) and the preferred one.
  • The web password, if it is 8 to 64 characters long. If it is not imported, the web interface stays open until you set one with WebPassword.

The import reads the settings layout of Tasmota 15.5.0.2. Settings from another version, or settings that are damaged, are skipped, and the device starts its setup network newmota-XXXXXX instead, as described in First Steps. Tasmota's settings files stay where they are; Newmota does not change them.

ESP32-H2, ESP32-C61 and ESP32-S31 are not supported by the import. ESP32-P4 stores the imported credentials, but its Newmota application has no Wi-Fi yet.

docs.title: 3b. Switch over a cable
docs.text:
Follow Install & Update Firmware: take a full backup with make backup first, then make flash, or use the Web Flasher. Then connect the device to Wi-Fi as described in First Steps.

The backup keeps the whole flash, Tasmota included, so you can write it back later.

docs.title: 4. Set the device up again
docs.text:
Paste the values you noted in step 1 on the Newmota console, for example:

Template {"NAME":"My Plug","GPIO":[...],"FLAG":0,"BASE":1}
Module 0
MqttHost 192.168.1.10
MqttUser mqttuser
MqttPassword <your password>
Topic myplug

Then check the hardware with Power1 on or Dimmer 50. Details are in Setting Up Your Device Hardware and MQTT & Telemetry.

docs.title: After an over-the-air switch
docs.text:
Tasmota's Safeboot stays on the device:

  • Restart 3, or Restart into Safeboot on the Firmware Update page, starts it. Its web page accepts a newer Newmota .bin or a Tasmota .bin, so you can go back to Tasmota the same way you came.
  • Tasmota's Safeboot keeps its own copy of the Wi-Fi settings. Wi-Fi changes you make in Newmota do not reach it, but its recovery access point stays available.
  • Upgrade 1 needs a Newmota Safeboot and reports Native update path unavailable on a switched device. A factory flash over a cable installs the Newmota Safeboot.

docs.title: Install & Update Firmware
docs.text:
This page gets Newmota onto your hardware: a backup of the original firmware first, the first install over a USB/serial cable or from the browser, updates later on, and watching the device boot. If your device already runs Newmota and you just want to use it, skip to First Steps.

No firmware yet? Build it first. Moving a device from Tasmota? See Switching From Tasmota.

docs.title: 1. Back Up First
docs.text:
Before the first install, read the device's whole flash into a file. With it you can put the original firmware back later.

# Show the connected chip, its security state, flash identity and size.
make probe ENV=esp32c2-2m

# Save the whole flash. Existing files are never replaced.
make backup ENV=esp32c2-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001 OUTPUT=backup.bin

Keep the backup outside build/firmware/. On AmebaD, probe and backup are not available yet.

docs.title: From the browser
docs.text: The Web Flasher writes a factory package from the browser, without a build environment: load newmota-<environment>-<version>-factory.zip from the build directory, connect the device and write. It writes the same regions and refuses the same cases as make flash-only, backs up the whole flash first (on by default), and opens a serial monitor afterwards. It covers Beken, Bouffalo, AmebaD, the ESP32 family and the Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040 and RP2350, over USB in BOOTSEL mode), in a desktop Chromium browser.

docs.title: Over a cable
docs.text:
# Build, package, probe, flash, verify and reset.
make flash ENV=esp32c2-2m

# The same, then open the serial console.
make flash-monitor ENV=esp32c2-2m

Every flash command checks the package manifest and its hashes before it opens the device.

Choosing the port: with one USB/serial adapter connected, it is picked automatically. With several, a menu opens (arrow keys; r refreshes the list), before the long build starts. PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001 sets it directly, for scripts.

ESP32BekenBouffaloPicoAmebaD 
make flash ENV=esp32c3-4m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

A device with more flash than the package gets a larger filesystem; a smaller one is refused. ESP32-S3 boards use the chip's built-in USB port, the ser variants UART0. See ESP32 Devices.

# Connect the programmer to the module's UART1/download pins.
make backup ENV=cb2s-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001 OUTPUT=cb2s-stock.bin
make flash ENV=cb2s-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

# XH-CB3S (BK7238) has its own environment; do not use cb3s for it.
make backup ENV=xh-cb3s PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001 OUTPUT=xh-cb3s-stock.bin
make flash ENV=xh-cb3s PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

The first operation must be the complete backup: it keeps the original bootloader and metadata. A flash starts with fresh Newmota settings; RF calibration and device identity are kept. Beken has no Newmota Safeboot; recovery means a stock OTA or a wired flash.

Tested so far: the XH-CB3S core stack. Update retention and recovery are open. Details

make backup ENV=bl602-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001 OUTPUT=bl602-stock.bin
make flash ENV=bl602-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

Tested so far: factory write and boot on BL602. Storage, the browser UI, recovery and updates are open; BL618DG is untested. Details

make backup ENV=pico2-w PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001 OUTPUT=pico2w-stock.bin
make flash ENV=pico2-w PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

The board must be in BOOTSEL mode. A running Newmota image usually switches to it by itself; otherwise hold BOOTSEL while connecting.

Tested so far: a Pico 2 W smoke test. Backup/restore and recovery are open. Details

# Enter UART download mode when prompted, then reset the board
# by hand after verification.
make flash ENV=bw16-2m PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

Tested so far: factory write, storage and Wi-Fi on BW16. Updates and recovery are open. Details

docs.title: Over the network
docs.text:
Set the address of an image on your network, then start the update:

> OtaUrl http://192.168.1.10:8000/firmware.bin
{"OtaUrl":"http://192.168.1.10:8000/firmware.bin"}

> Upgrade 1
{"Upgrade":"Downloading"}

> Upgrade
{"Upgrade":"Active","Bytes":524288,"Total":1048576}

Upgrade 1 loads the image over plain HTTP from a server that sends its length; HTTPS, redirects and chunked transfers are refused. Upgrade shows the progress.

In the browser:

  • Firmware Update page (normal web UI): shows the running version and build. "Update from URL" saves OtaUrl and starts Upgrade 1, polling Upgrade once a second while the page is open and an update is active (platforms that download inside Safeboot report the handoff and restart). The update-channel card has no backend yet and stays visibly unavailable.
  • Safeboot Recovery Web: On ESP-IDF, Bouffalo, AmebaD, and Pico targets, type Restart 3 on the console to boot into the dedicated Safeboot recovery image. Navigate to http://<device-ip>/ to access the authenticated recovery page and upload a new application image chunk-by-chunk directly from your browser. The normal web UI's Firmware Update page does the same handoff for you: "Upload firmware file" runs Restart 3 and then shows the recovery page. Safeboot requires a configured WebPassword and refuses access without it, so the page warns when none is set.
  • Beken Dedicated Web Updater: On BK7231N and BK7238 targets, normal application firmware embeds a compact root page containing device status, console, LittleFS browser, and a native RBL updater.

A device that was switched from Tasmota over the air keeps Tasmota's Safeboot; see Switching From Tasmota.

docs.title: Over a cable
docs.text:
make update ENV=esp32c2-2m

make update is the quick cycle while you tinker: it rebuilds and writes only the application. The bootloader, Safeboot and your files and settings stay as they are; on Bouffalo, Pico and AmebaD a device that is in Safeboot stays there. On Beken it writes the stock OTA area, which overlaps the filesystem, so your files may be erased (Wi-Fi credentials are kept). On AmebaD, enter UART download mode when prompted and reset by hand afterwards. On Pico, the board must be in BOOTSEL mode.

make update is not the signed remote update. What it writes on each platform is described in Build System Internals.

docs.title: 4. Watching the Device
docs.text:
make monitor ENV=esp32c2-2m

MONITOR_PORT selects a different logging UART for the two -monitor commands; MONITOR_BAUD overrides its speed. BAUD overrides programming speed (or monitor speed for standalone make monitor). On Beken the runtime console is UART1 (see Beken devices); typed characters are not echoed.

Default speeds:

Platform Upload baud Console baud AmebaD 230400 115200 Beken 1500000 115200 Bouffalo 500000 2000000 ESP-IDF, Pico SDK Programmer default 115200

docs.title: Command Reference
docs.text:
Command Action make probe ENV=<env> Inspects connected chip identity, flash ID, security state, and physical flash capacity. make backup ENV=<env> OUTPUT=backup.bin Reads full physical flash memory and saves a raw recovery backup outside build/firmware/. Existing files are never replaced. make flash ENV=<env> Builds, packages, probes, flashes, verifies, and resets the target device. make update ENV=<env> Short wired dev cycle: rebuilds and writes only the application region (see below). make flash-only PACKAGE=<path> Flashes an existing development factory package manifest without compiling code. make monitor ENV=<env> Opens interactive serial console monitor. make flash-monitor ENV=<env> Flashes device and automatically connects serial monitor with post-flash reset. make flash-only-monitor PACKAGE=<path> Flashes an existing package, then connects the monitor.

make flash-only writes an existing package without building:

make flash-only PACKAGE=build/firmware/esp32c2-2m/<version>/manifest.json
make flash-only-monitor PACKAGE=build/firmware/esp32c2-2m/<version>/manifest.json

docs.title: Raspberry Pi Pico W & Pico 2 W
docs.text: Newmota on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W (RP2350, 4 MiB flash) and original Raspberry Pi Pico W (RP2040, 2 MiB flash) using the official Pico SDK v2.3.1. For flashing you put the board in BOOTSEL mode; day-to-day use is identical to every other device — browser and console.

docs.title: Native Build & Toolchain Integration
docs.text: The Raspberry Pi build adapter (tools/newmota/platforms/pico/build.py) coordinates native CMake builds against upstream Pico SDK:

docs.title: Managed Toolchain & Programmer
docs.text:
• Cross-Compiler: Pinned Arm GNU bare-metal toolchain (xpack-arm-none-eabi-gcc v14.2.1-1.1), managed under ~/.newmota/tools/arm-none-eabi/ and shared with the Beken target.
  • Programmer Utility: Pinned official picotool v2.3.1, managed under ~/.newmota/tools/pico-sdk/picotool-2.3.1/.
  • SDK Version Declaration: config/sdk/pico-sdk.toml pinning commit 079c6f39023649b154152db30f1d781e884879bc.

docs.title: Native Lifecycle Stages
docs.text:
1. Configure: Invokes CMake (Unix Makefiles) pointing to src/platform/pico-sdk/native/CMakeLists.txt with target platform (rp2350 or rp2040) and board (pico2_w or pico_w).
  2. Build: Compiles application core C++ sources and Pico SDK native drivers into build/work/<env>/native/.
  3. Compilation Database: Generates compile_commands.json for IDE integration via make clangd ENV=pico2-w or make clangd ENV=pico-w.
  4. Post-Build Artifacts: Produces binary output files:
  5. newmota.elf: Debug binary with complete symbol tables.
  6. newmota.bin: Raw flashable binary image.
  7. newmota.uf2: Drag-and-drop USB bootloader binary.

docs.title: Building Pico Firmware
docs.text:
# Explicit toolchain and SDK setup
make setup PLATFORM=pico

# Build Pico 2 W (RP2350, 4 MiB)
make pico2-w

# Build original Pico W (RP2040, 2 MiB)
make pico-w

The pico2-w target is also included in the routine cross-platform test matrix executed by make test.

Application environments declare their companion safeboot dependencies (safeboot: pico2-w-safeboot or safeboot: pico-w-safeboot); the pipeline builds the safeboot image first, then the application. Each role links at its own slot base with linker-enforced budgets.

docs.title: RP2350 4 MiB Layout (4m-rp2350.json)
docs.text:
The RP2350 uses picotool JSON partition definitions on the RP2350 boot ROM image-chain API. Safeboot starts at flash offset zero and embeds the resident partition table; the table-free application sits behind it and is linked at XIP_BASE, because the ROM rolls the chosen flash partition into the runtime window when it chains. The resolver pins this geometry exactly, so an unreviewed edit fails closed.

Region Offset Size Content Safeboot 0x000000 0x0D0000 Recovery image; owns the embedded native partition table Application 0x0D0000 0x2D2000 Normal firmware (table-free launchable image) Data 0x3A2000 0x05B000 Marker sector + LittleFS ├─ Sticky-boot marker (platform-owned) 0x3A2000 4 KiB Power-cycle-persistent Safeboot request, outside the LittleFS geometry └─ LittleFS 0x3A3000 0x05A000 Filesystem (native adapter in src/platform/pico-sdk/filesystem.cpp) BTstack reserve 0x3FD000 0x002000 Reserved E10 last-sector reserve 0x3FF000 4 KiB Preserved

Both images use secure-only executable permissions with independent (unlinked) slots; the TBYB IMAGE_DEF bit stays clear on both so factory and normal boots just work. A rendered standalone table ships in the package as a reference only and is not flashed.

docs.title: RP2040 2 MiB Layout (2m-rp2040.json)
docs.text: Region Offset Size Content Safeboot 0x000000 0x0C0000 Recovery image Application 0x0C0000 0x12F000 Normal firmware Boot marker 0x1EF000 4 KiB Sticky-boot marker LittleFS 0x1F0000 0x010000 (64 KiB) Filesystem (cached reads, normal writes enabled)

docs.title: Boot selection and updates
docs.text: Restart 3 arms the marker and the entry point chains into Safeboot before any service starts; a failed chain clears the request so a corrupt Safeboot image cannot reboot-loop. The wired update rebuilds the single application image and writes only the application slot after validating the installed Newmota table; Safeboot, LittleFS, the marker, and the reserves are untouched (the marker is preserved, so a device in Safeboot stays there).

docs.title: Storage & Filesystem Status
docs.text:
• Serial Console: Operates over native USB CDC (pico_stdio_usb); uses the common serial monitor.
  • Filesystem Adapter: Native LittleFS block-device adapter (src/platform/pico-sdk/filesystem.cpp) over the dedicated update-preserved region behind the marker sector. Settings are kept there and not duplicated into vendor stores.
  • Boot selection: Platform-owned marker sector (src/platform/pico-sdk/boot_select.h), outside the LittleFS geometry.

docs.title: Wired Operations
docs.text:
make probe ENV=pico2-w PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001
make backup ENV=pico2-w PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001 OUTPUT=pico2w-stock.bin
make flash ENV=pico2-w PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001
make update ENV=pico2-w PORT=/dev/cu.usbserial-0001

The factory package carries both FW images and an empty LittleFS image. Factory provisioning performs identity/capacity preflight and can replace a virgin or foreign table; application-only updates additionally require the exact installed Newmota table and verify each component by read-back. picotool operations need the board in BOOTSEL mode; a running Newmota image usually reboots into BOOTSEL by itself, otherwise hold BOOTSEL while connecting or resetting the board. UF2 files remain native build artifacts rather than package components.

Note

picotool file-model operations on large binaries (info, uf2 convert) were observed throwing std::bad_alloc on the macOS host build. Build-time partition embedding (ELF path) and all host-side byte-level checks are unaffected; device-path operations are hardware testing scope.

docs.title: Optional Wireless Features
docs.text:
The CYW43439 provides BLE 5.2, and the firmware can use it, but no checked-in Pico profile selects BLE or Matter:

  • USE_BLE / USE_BLE_SENSORS compile the Pico SDK BTstack backend and native sensor decoding. Pico W/RP2040 needs a separate variant; the adapter is compile-tested only. See Bluetooth & BLE Sensors.
  • USE_MATTER (and optionally USE_MATTER_BLE) runs on RP2350 only and needs at least 4 MiB flash, which the Pico 2 W provides. RP2040 is rejected. See Matter.

Enable either in a personal build configuration and test on your board; compilation does not establish radio operation or Wi-Fi coexistence.

docs.title: Hardware testing
docs.text:
An exact Pico 2 W smoke test has passed: factory write with read-back verification, reset/USB CDC reconnect, LittleFS mount/read, settings persistence, Wi-Fi/NTP startup, HTTP, browser UI, and web-console operation.

Still open: backup/restore, recovery, interrupted-update behavior, and broader testing. What each wired operation writes is described in Build System Internals.

docs.title: Supported Devices
docs.text:
Newmota runs on real consumer hardware across five microcontroller families — ESP32, Raspberry Pi Pico (Pico W and Pico 2 W), Bouffalo, Beken, and AmebaD — so one familiar interface (web UI + console commands) covers plugs, switches, dimmers, lights, and sensors regardless of the chip inside.

All platform implementations use their native SDKs without an Arduino compatibility layer. Select an environment that matches your chip and board; the platform guides describe the available flashing and update methods.

docs.text: Platform Microcontrollers Native SDK Example environments ESP32 ESP32, C2, C3, C5, C6, C61, S2, S3, S31, P4, P4X, H2 ESP-IDF v5.5 / v6.1 esp32c2-2m Raspberry Pi Pico RP2040 (Pico W), RP2350 (Pico 2 W) Pico SDK v2.3.1 pico-w, pico2-w Bouffalo BL602, BL616, BL618DG (low priority, untested); BL702 planned BouffaloSDK v2.3.34 bl602-2m, bl602-4m, bl616dk, bl618dgdk Beken BK7231T, BK7231N, BK7238, BK7251, BK7252, BK7252N framework-beken-bdk v3.0.78 cb2s-2m, cb3s, wb2s, xh-cb3s, generic-bk7252-2m, generic-bk7252n-2m AmebaD RTL8720D / RTL8720DN Ameba RTOS-D bw16-2m

docs.title: Optional Features by Platform

docs.title: Flash Memory Admission Gate
docs.text:
Sub-2 MiB Physical Flash Rule

Newmota requires a minimum physical flash size of 2 MiB across all target microcontrollers. 1 MiB hardware (such as ESP8266 or RTL8710AF/BN) is outside the scope of this project; for the ESP8266, Tasmota is the place to go.

docs.title: Profile Distribution
docs.text:
• Compact Profile (2 MiB): Default profile for 2 MiB targets (pico-w, esp32c2-2m, cb2s-2m, bl602-2m, bw16-2m). Includes mandatory device-hosted web server + essential UI (HTTP+Gzip on port 80), bounded plain MQTT client and telemetry, LittleFS storage, and serial console. Note: WPA3-SAE is omitted on 2 MiB ESP images to fit flash constraints.
  • Standard Profile (4 MiB): Enabled by default on 4 MiB+ targets (pico2-w, esp32c3-4m, esp32s3-qio-qspi, bl602-4m, bl616dk, bl618dgdk). Serves the web UI over HTTP+Gzip on port 80 by default (set USE_WEB_HTTPS: true for HTTPS), and includes the BearSSL crypto module, single language pack, Berry scripting engine, and hardened session security.
  • Large Profile (ESP32-P4, ESP32-S31, esp32s3-qio-opi-8m-8m): HTTPS on port 443 with Brotli-compressed assets and a per-device self-signed certificate by default. Display (USE_DISPLAY, USE_DISPLAY_QSPI, USE_UNIVERSAL_TOUCH), LVGL (USE_LVGL), and I2S audio (USE_I2S) are optional features selected in a personal build on any platform with enough flash.
  • Safeboot Profile: Minimal standalone recovery image with bounded plain MQTT client, and stripped authenticated HTTP+Gzip recovery page with a bounded application-image updater.
